When the horn imitation mingles with the inspection bell, workers in helmets are the first to lose their bearings. That same evening, the flock descends on the basket and scatters the tools. After the third horn blast, the air above the bridge locks into a single call pattern, entangling the basket and schoolchildren’s umbrellas in the same wind.

### Combat and Response
Attaching a counter-directional noise generator to the tower’s base throws the horn imitation gathered by the ruling pair one beat off. On that missed beat, the flock splits in two in midair. If the generator starts after the third horn blast, claws still blanket the work basket, and the day shift postpones roof work for a day.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
The day-shift foreman must decide whether to publish the three-blast pattern in the work log or keep it as a call known only to the roof watch. Once published, the communal roost will learn it overnight, and it cannot be taken back. If it is kept secret, a new shift worker will draw the flock’s expectation of food to the same basket. G02-SC1 also records the cost of leaving the human safety call unavailable for several days while the pattern is retired.

### Scenario Connections
The three horn blasts of G02-SC1 become the clock for the whole roost through this pair’s bodies. The misclassification in G02-SC2 and the convergence at the bridge in G02-SC3 leave behind a night when that clock overlaps with human calls.

/monster_contents/M002/entries/7/bestiar.en: The scout 'Shadowwing' is a stealthy observer that counts only helmet outlines and cannot read electronic content. It passes its report to the breeding pair by call, providing coordinates for the afternoon dive.

/monster_contents/M002/entries/7/prose.en:
### Role and Body
The metallic feathers of its thin wings scatter the surrounding light, making its shape hard to see when it clings between two buildings. Flying low during the school commute, it watches the line of people and passes their positions to the breeding pair by call only after sunset.

### Origin
It is one of a brood sent on the ruling pair’s first reconnaissance early in G02-SC1. Its stealth flight gives the roost an information advantage, but it cannot read electronic content.

### Habitat
It darts between buildings and over disused tracks, remaining concealed by day to count the people in line and climbing to the top only to report at night. It must avoid high-voltage noise to maintain its concealment.

### Needs and Economy
It pecks at small insects and scraps of insulation, offering its gathered position calls to the pair to keep the whole roost’s feeding clock running. If reconnaissance is interrupted, the dive coordinates go astray, leaving only the school wall more dangerous.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
Flying through narrow gaps often tears its wings, which are regenerated by the call pattern at the tower top. If regeneration is delayed, the morning flight path goes unused and the calls near the school spread a day late.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
Following the pair’s instructions, it gathers positions only and keeps its flight path separate from those of attackers and relays. The order of reports establishes an information hierarchy within the roost.

### Escalating Threat
One morning, it counts only helmet outlines while concealed. When other scouts gather, they imitate the inspection bell together, confusing people below the wall. Once that imitation reaches the tower top, the afternoon dive targets the correct school gate.

### Combat and Response
If the reconnaissance coordinates reach the breeding pair before the school commute ends, the afternoon dive is redrawn around the school wall. Hanging a visual screening cloth across the flight path between two buildings makes the light-scattering feathers lose their concealment and cuts off daytime reports. If one wing briefly reflects light whenever the cloth flutters, the number of people taking the detour below the wall does not increase that day.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
The school-commute marshal sets a limit from the outset: test the screening cloth for only three days and take it down on the fourth morning. If the dives leave the wall clear within those three days, the scout’s calls remain directed only toward the tower. Exceed the limit, and young birds begin testing a new roost on the stair handrail. In the week when G02-SC3’s communal bridge roost opens, even those three days overlap with the umbrella procession.

### Scenario Connections
The umbrella procession in G02-SC3 uses the same wall as this scout’s flight path. The horn learning in G02-SC1 and the misclassification of calls in G02-SC2 create the route by which reconnaissance coordinates enter human work logs.

/monster_contents/M002/entries/8/bestiar.en: The attacker 'Ironbeak' is built to descend and split concrete joints. It dives only when the pair’s command and reconnaissance coordinates coincide, and it keeps its route separate from the relay’s.

/monster_contents/M002/entries/8/prose.en:
### Role and Body
Its metallic beak splits concrete joints, while its short wings build speed as it drops from roof height. After sighting a target railing from the tower top, it descends in one plunge and cuts across an exposed pedestrian stretch.

### Origin
Amid the sparks and transformer noise of G02-SC1, birds with hard beaks took on the attack role. Since then, the roost’s physical pressure has been measured by the number of their dives.

### Habitat
It waits on high roofs, then strikes alternately at the catenary and ground-level railings when coordinates arrive. The difference in height gives its descent force, so daytime pedestrians and nighttime repair crews occupy the same vertical line.

### Needs and Economy
It delivers insects and protein gained after a dive to the roost, and the call pattern at the tower top repairs wear on its beak. When dives miss and it returns empty-beaked more often, the breeding pair’s feeding clock falters.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
Its beak wears down with every dive and cannot split joints without regular regeneration. The number of times a bird has been regenerated changes the order of attackers within the roost.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It dives only when the pair’s dive command coincides with reconnaissance coordinates. It does not share a flight path with relay birds, so its descent follows a separate line.

### Escalating Threat
Just after the horn imitation, the first dive strikes a railing. The impact of the beak widens a crack and exposes insulation. When another attacker joins the same vertical line, umbrellas in the school passage fold all at once, and the waiting line stretches to the bridge entrance.

### Combat and Response
The dive breaks into a glide before the concrete joint, and the tip of the beak merely grazes the railing. This is the result of the bridge repair team hanging acoustic screens at staggered heights along the descent path. If the screens are lower than the catenary, the beak tears the insulation, leaving pedestrian injuries and a season of short-circuit inspections.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
On the roof where the horns of G02-SC1 raised expectations of food, the bridge team and the Haeryun Mobile Gate leave only one lane as a dive corridor. If they keep the corridor fixed until spring breeding, the pedestrian path stays open, but the work basket must avoid that lane. If they remove the lane, the nest radius will not be redrawn until the next breeding season. The corridor disappears only when both parties remove the markers together.

### Scenario Connections
G02-SC1 supplies the call pattern that triggers a dive. The false-alarm week of G02-SC2 and the sea-wind breeding of G02-SC3 set the calendar for redrawing the corridor markers.

/monster_contents/M002/entries/9/bestiar.en: The relay 'Linkfeather' is an echo-bodied bird that carries the inspection bell’s overtones to the next tower. It stays out of scout and attack flight paths; only the clarity of its echo determines which tower takes priority.

/monster_contents/M002/entries/9/prose.en:
### Role and Body
The copying organ in its throat and the arrangement of its wings carry the inspection bell’s overtones to the next tower. It travels at mid-tower height; near communications equipment, the bell’s echo speeds up by one beat.

### Origin
In G02-SC1, the ruling pair selected birds to send call patterns farther, and they divided this relay role among them. The roost’s stable sense of time depends on the quality of their echoes.

### Habitat
It moves constantly between the catenary crossing of the Wangsimni United Line Succession State and the factory towers, keeping to the optimal height. During weeks when insulation is replaced, that height overlaps with the work basket.

### Needs and Economy
The energy it uses to copy calls comes from the pair’s calls at the tower top. The clearer the echo, the more the flock moves at one time, tangling the inspection crew’s routes.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
It frequently adjusts the angle of its feathers to match the overtones. If they tear, it presses against a neighboring relay bird and borrows its angle to recover. A bird whose feather angle fails is pushed back in the roost’s copying order.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It only carries the pair’s call patterns and does not enter scout or attack flight paths. The clarity of its echo determines that day’s priority tower.

### Escalating Threat
When an overtone drifts slightly, the times in the work log are the first to become unreliable. As the drift grows, the flock lands on the wrong tower and tires while waiting for tools. An amplified false echo then binds neighboring roosts to the same bell sound, leaving three towers empty at once when a single inspection bell rings.

### Combat and Response
Silence just one inspection-bell overtone imitated by the relay bird’s throat organ first. If the overtone remains, the next tower takes the false echo as its work schedule. The insulation inspection crew climbs an empty tower, while insulation on the main line remains stripped that same week.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Before the false outage classification of G02-SC2 sounds, the Haeryun Mobile Gate, the Railway Successor Bureau’s track workers, and the alley bellkeeper agree to leave just one keeper in charge of the relay roost. During a week when the keeper changes, human hands redirect the inspection bell’s echo route; if they leave the post unattended, the call is once again taken as a sign of an impending outage. One mistaken work order leads to a gap in insulation at another tower, and the track workers’ shift bears that debt.

### Scenario Connections
The false outage of G02-SC2 tests the quality of this relay’s echo. The horn pattern of G02-SC1 and the communal roost of G02-SC3 use the same tower height during the week of the keeper’s changeover.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/0/bestiar.en: Fine-Wire Weaver 'Sheathing Hand' is a weaving body that coils stripped wire into a cup. It gives no orders; when the cup grows light, it starts by pulling screws from the railing.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/0/prose.en:
### Role and Body
In the roof gutters of the Yeongdeungpo Line Standards Alliance factory lives a weaving body that pulls stripped fine wires out with its beak and coils them into a cup. Its claws are worn from holding fiber scraps in place. When the coiling stops, the breeding pair strips substitute material from the school-passage railing, lengthening the morning journey to school.

### Origin
One spring, when the Sinjeong Wheel Guild stripped wire sheathing all at once, fragments piled up in a roof gutter. One bird began coiling them, remembering only the feel of copper and the springiness of fiber. It could not read the content of the transmissions; only the pairing of shine and softness remained, and the habit hardened into a fictive weaving task.

### Habitat
By day it hides the cup in a bracket's shade, descending to the edges of the sheathing only in the evening, when work noise subsides. During breeding season, the cup moves to a windward spot toward the bridge. In weeks when the sea wind from XT02 West Sea Granary Bulge shakes the fine wires, a low arm of the Nanji remnant tower serves as a temporary coiling site.

### Needs and Economy
Maintaining the nest takes a palmful each of stripped fine wire and fiber every week. If Haeryun moves collection forward, materials run short and railings and signposts are stripped. If the sheathing is left in place, the cup thickens, but the risk of a short circuit rises and available transmission minutes are lost.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
If rain loosens the outer ring, it recoils it that evening; it adds just one layer to the inner ring per season. Evenings spent coiling mean less insect gathering, so the breeding pair on the same tower relies more heavily on leftover protein from the market.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
The weaving body does not give orders. When the cup grows light, it is the first to move toward material. The breeding pair adjusts its defensive radius by watching that movement alone, while a young helper merely carries fiber in its beak and never learns the coiling sequence.

### Escalating Threat
At first, only the fragments in the roof gutter disappear. When materials run short, screws vanish from the school-route railing. In a week when the cup is empty, even the signposts are stripped, increasing the number of people forced to detour and making access by work basket more dangerous.

### Combat and Response
Once the fine-wire ring of the nest cup completes three turns in a week, the beak stops stripping the school railing. If the replacement crew misses the window for deliberately leaving a handful of fragments beside the cup, the ring remains loose come morning. When the cup is empty, the same beak pulls screws from school-route signposts, increasing the number of people detouring by day.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
During replacement week, one member of the sheathing replacement crew chooses whether to leave fine-wire fragments beside the cup or collect them all. Leaving them preserves the railing, but the expectation of food associated with G02-SC1's horns shifts toward the cup, making access by basket dangerous for one more day. Sweeping up every fragment lightens G02-SC1's work basket, but the railing screws are the first to go missing.

### Scenario Connections
G02-SC1 records whether the window for leaving fine-wire fragments opens in the same week as the horn pattern. G02-SC2's false blackout coincides with insulator contamination on towers with thick cups, and G02-SC3's airspace above the bridge opens as a communal roost only after the coiling site moves to the railing.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/1/bestiar.en: Spark Forager 'Insect Neck' is a foraging body that chases insects drawn by trolley-wire sparks and mistakes the backs of gloved hands for insects, pecking them. Even when the breeding pair begins its dives, it does not leave the crossing until the insect cloud disperses.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/1/prose.en:
### Role and Body
At the trolley-wire crossing of the Wangsimni Union Line Succession State, the foraging body that chases nocturnal insects drawn by sparks has neck feathers scorched by ions. Its beak cannot distinguish the back of a gloved hand at the edge of a work basket from an insect, and the resulting wound delays the welding shift by an hour.

### Origin
As factory waste heat and overhead-wire sparks produced insect clouds night after night, one bird learned to follow the basket and pick off only the insects exposed there. It was not drawn to the equipment itself: it linked the recurring work noise, sheathing fragments, and glinting insects into one trail, and that trail became its foraging role.

### Habitat
After sunset it circles only within twenty meters beneath the trolley wire; by day it rests in the shade of the crossing's steel poles. When a maintenance basket rises, it compares the basket's height with the insect lamp's. In weeks when the sea wind pushes insects toward the western waterfront, it briefly moves to the bridge's lower chord.

### Needs and Economy
For foraging to continue, the nocturnal insects must be concentrated away from basket height. If the lamp overlaps the basket, both gloves and wire sheathing get torn; if the lamp is turned off, the foraging body descends toward leftover protein at the market and disrupts the loading alleys.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
The day after rain, it rubs its scorched neck feathers clean and dry in a sand bath, and a broken beak tip regrows within three days. If it chooses a school playground rather than trolley-wire gravel for its bath, daytime school bells mingle with its foraging memory, increasing mistaken approaches the next night.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
The forager does not direct the basket; it follows only the insect lamp's height. Even when the breeding pair begins diving, this body does not leave the crossing before the insect cloud disperses. A young helper picks up only fallen insects and carries them to the nest.

### Escalating Threat
On the first day, only the insects around the lamp diminish. If the lamp and basket remain at the same height, holes appear in gloves. If that continues for three days, the welding schedule slips and the foraging route spills toward the school wall by day.

### Combat and Response
If the insect lamp beneath the trolley-wire sparks remains level with the basket, the forager pecks the backs of gloved hands first. Lowering the lamp by one length to the arm of a disused steel tower separates the insect cloud from the basket. Basket claw marks disappear only on nights when the lamp is moved to the disused tower; a shift that fails to move it uses an extra pair of welding gloves.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
The night basket crew and daytime school-route guides share authority to move feeding to hours without horns. Keeping G02-SC1's horn pattern in the daytime protects the line of children, but the night welders face both sparks and beaks. The welders bear that night's fatigue, while the line of children below the school wall is shorter by day.

### Scenario Connections
G02-SC1 notes whether the cost of moving food to a horn-free night accumulates on the welding shift. G02-SC2's relocation of the insect lamp draws this foraging body's remembered height toward the disused steel tower, and during G02-SC3's sea-wind week, insects at the crossing mix with those beneath the bridge.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/2/bestiar.en: Insulator Fouler 'White Rim' is a defecating body more inclined to settle than to dive. The real cause of transmission shutdown is not its call but the thickness of the film on the insulator cap.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/2/prose.en:
### Role and Body
The contamination-specialized body that perches atop the insulator caps of the Nanji remnant transmission tower and leaves a white rim of droppings is more inclined to settle than to dive. Sunlight on the film weakens insulation, shaving available transmission time in ten-minute increments until control shuts it down.

### Origin
As the cycle of droppings contaminating insulators came to affect communications time, only birds that chose caps for their warmth and roughness remained. People tried to read blackouts in the calls, but the real cause was the film's thickness; that misunderstanding fixed its fictive contamination role.

### Habitat
It stays on the southern arm, where daytime sun warms the caps, briefly moving to a warm factory-roof vent on rainy nights. Vibration keeps it from sitting long on the insulators at the Wangsimni Union rail overhead-wire crossing. In weeks of strong sea winds, ceramic sleeves on the bridge cables serve as an alternative perch.

### Needs and Economy
To sustain the film, a cap must remain unwashed and rough for several days, allowing insect husks to adhere to it. If the cleaning team keeps its appointed window, transmission minutes return, but the fouling body moves to the paint on the school-passage railing and soils the detour signs.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
The white rim becomes visible in three days and attracts sparks within a week. If rain washes away only part of it, the bird returns to the same cap to restore its thickness; it avoids a fully cleaned cap for three days.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
The fouling bird does not call the flock with its voice; it chooses only the warmth of the cap. Even when the breeding pair defends the tower, this body does not leave the lower row of insulators. H02 Seorin's sound-pattern record can easily mistake this settled behavior for diving.

### Escalating Threat
By the time the white rim is visible, transmission minutes are already falling. Delay cleaning by a day and sparks fly in the afternoon; if control shuts down without a visual inspection, both the factory roof and rail crossing close.

### Combat and Response
When accumulated droppings form a white rim in sunlight on an insulator cap, available transmission time has already fallen by ten minutes. If the crew takes only a brush and distilled water up during the short morning cleaning window and removes the film, sparks will not carry into that afternoon. A tower that misses the cleaning window spits sparks that same week's afternoon, and control presses the shutdown button before a visual inspection.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Before Seorin reports a diving call as a warning of a blackout, the insulator-cleaning team first enters the film's thickness in the ledger. Recording it keeps transmission running for ten more minutes, but draws cleaning personnel away from another tower that morning. Omit the ledger entry, and G02-SC2's false blackout closes the factory roof and rail crossing on the same afternoon.

### Scenario Connections
In G02-SC2, the opening for a false blackout appears when the film-thickness ledger takes precedence over call classification. During G02-SC1's horn week, the cleaning window overlaps work noise and is postponed. On G02-SC3's bridge sleeves, the sea wind dries the rim and expands the contaminated area.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/3/bestiar.en: Breeding Defender 'Paired Radius' is a breeding pair that divides one tower into upper and lower territory. This division does not carry over to the communal roost; if one bird is absent, only clashes with neighboring pairs increase.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/3/prose.en:
### Role and Body
In spring, the bodies of a breeding pair guarding the upper and lower parts of a steel tower establish a radius. The male above reads the outline of a helmet first, while the female below reads the angle of a pole; their dives from two directions target the edges of a work basket at once.

### Origin
A fictive division of labor, in which two birds perch on separate halves of a tower, grew from large-billed crows' breeding-season territorial defense. Repeated sparks and worker appearances taught them the radius's extent. If one bird disappeared, a neighboring pair tested the vacant spot and clashes increased.

### Habitat
The spring radius centers on the upper and lower arms of the factory-roof steel tower. Outside breeding season, the division dissolves and the birds join a communal roost. They patrol above the bridge and school passage but do not nest there; when a helmet enters the radius, they end the patrol and return to the tower.

### Needs and Economy
Maintaining the radius requires nesting material and insects, as well as intervals when helmets and poles are out of sight. If the basket crosses the radius every day, defensive labor consumes time needed to carry food and the chicks lose weight. If the basket never rises, damage to sheathing goes unattended and short circuits worsen.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
The lower bird incubating the eggs changes places only once every two days; the upper bird carries food during that time. It preens torn feathers only in the shade of a canopy. If the work platform below the tower's middle is used as shade, the angle of its next dive is redrawn around that platform.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
Only the pair divides the radius; young helpers merely add warning calls. The division does not carry over to the communal roost. If one breeding bird is absent, a neighboring pair tests the vacant perch, increasing territorial clashes.

### Escalating Threat
When the outline of a helmet brushes the edge of the radius, only the calls change. Once it enters, dives begin from both directions. If the canopy covers only the tower's middle, the upper bird's beak severs a basket strap and parts fall.

### Combat and Response
When the breeding pair guards the upper and lower tower simultaneously, a helmet outline entering their radius triggers dives from two directions. Hanging canopies on the upper arm and the middle at staggered times disrupts their sightlines, scattering their glides toward the railing. Wrapping a canopy around only the tower's middle blocks the lower beak, while the upper beak tears the basket's edge.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Within the spring radius, Haeryun's maneuver order reduces work-basket operations to a single line in exchange for recognizing the breeding pair's upper perch. If G02-SC1's new horn pattern is read as food within the radius, that recognition slows basket operations by a day. Drive the pair from the perch, and recognition will not return before the next breeding season; helmeted workers' scalps pay the price first.

### Scenario Connections
G02-SC1 records whether to recognize the upper perch or reduce basket operations when horns heighten the expectation of food inside the radius. G02-SC2's misclassification of calls reads the pair's warning calls as a blackout warning. During G02-SC3's sea-wind week, the radius briefly dissolves at the communal roost above the bridge.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/4/bestiar.en: Sound-Pattern Core 'Mixed Bells' is a temporary core body that echoes inspection bells learned at different towers above the bridge. It gives no orders, providing only a place where sound patterns converge; when the sea wind shifts, the circle disappears too.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/4/prose.en:
### Role and Body
When inspection bells learned by several families converge at one point above the Han River bridge, a core body appears that amplifies their mingling without a leader. The core synchronizes its wingbeats to echo the bells; at a single strike, the flock is already moving and the line behind the umbrellas backs up.

### Origin
The rule that a nonbreeding communal roost shares only sound patterns acquired a fictive twist: in a week when sea winds and breeding coincide, bells from different towers mingle at one bridge. The meaning of the transmissions remains unread; only the density of overlapping echoes remains, and that density creates a place for the core.

### Habitat
The core's place forms only within a thirty-meter circle above the transmission inspection hatch, and the circle vanishes when the sea wind shifts. Birds that learned their bells at the Yeongdeungpo Line roof and the Wangsimni Union crossing exchange them when they enter the circle, then scatter back to their original towers once the exchange is over that night.

### Needs and Economy
The core persists only when sea wind, breeding, and bells struck without a time offset coincide. Stagger the bells tower by tower and the core fades within three or four days. Refuse to stagger them, and the rear of the evacuation column remains at the railing, reducing the number who can pass.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
The core's coordinated behavior lasts no more than a week; when the sea wind changes, it must relearn its wing synchronization. Young birds that have not fully learned it call only at the circle's edge, and those edge calls widen the gaps in the line of umbrellas.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
The core gives no orders; it only provides a place where sound patterns converge. The breeding pairs' division of radii does not apply here. Even if H02 identifies a single leader, HC02 control records only the differences in bell-striking times.

### Escalating Threat
When bells from different towers join into one sound, the flock begins filling the circle. If synchronized bell strikes continue, the rear of the umbrella line stops. At the third accumulation, evacuees left at the railing stand beneath the dives, clutching their bags.

### Combat and Response
When inspection bells learned at different towers mingle above one bridge, a single bell already sets the flock in motion. Striking each tower's bell ten minutes apart makes the core's echo scatter a beat late. With the bells staggered by tower, the rear of the column makes it under the umbrellas; without staggering, evacuees at the rear remain at the railing.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
The Yeongdeungpo Line, Wangsimni Union, and Haeryun must enter the sea-wind week's communal roost in one ledger before they can divide up the new inspection-bell times. Doing so lowers the circle's density at the cost of several days of relearning. If the ledger remains blank, G02-SC3's bridge opens, but children and evacuees become new targets for dives.

### Scenario Connections
G02-SC3 records the week when sea wind and breeding coincide and the core appears as the highest threat level. If G02-SC1's horn pattern mixes into the core's sound pattern, the circle expands as far as the work basket. G02-SC2's misclassification reads the core's echo as a blackout warning.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/5/bestiar.en: Remnant-Tower Organ 'Crossbeam Tone' is a place where the crossbeam of the Sangam remnant tower and the wind form one body. With no leader, the birds read its low tone as the number of the arm on which to perch.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/5/prose.en:
### Role and Body
The moment a crossbeam of the Sangam remnant tower produces a low tone in the wind, the place-based organ formed by beam and wind becomes a set of roost coordinates. Several families read the tone, without a leader, as the number of the arm on which to perch. If the tone stops, droppings and diving birds descend together below the inspection hatch.

### Origin
After the transmission towers left at Sangam and Nanji came to serve as both nest and feeding ground, the crossbeam's resonance was learned as a safety signal. Not a genetic change but the recurring pairing of wind and insect lamps turned the place into an organ. That learning continued month by month until a demolition declaration was issued.

### Habitat
Outside breeding season, the middle arm of the Sangam remnant tower is the center; the Nanji side becomes active only briefly when the lamp is moved. During breeding season, the place's function weakens as pairs divide the tower into radii. In sea-wind weeks, the crossbeam tone becomes confused with the low tone of bridge cables.

### Needs and Economy
For the place to remain an organ, the crossbeam must not be demolished, and there must be room to move the insect lamp to Nanji. Fixing the lamp at the remnant tower lets a film of droppings close the transmission inspection hatch. Merely turning it off sends the families to the factory roof's waste heat, consuming the nighttime maintenance window.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
When the crossbeam's bolts loosen, its tone rises by one note and the coordinates shift; tightening them lowers it again. If the maintenance crew leaves the lamp on while tightening the bolts at night, the families learn that higher note as the new coordinates, making the next month's records wrong.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
The place is the center, and the families only share its tone; there is no leader. Even if H02 marks one heat source as the core, the control officer separately records the crossbeam arm number and lamp position.

### Escalating Threat
After the low tone repeats for three days, the perch arm becomes fixed. If the lamp cannot be moved to Nanji, droppings accumulate on the inspection-hatch cover, and dives in the same week keep the cover closed, causing one transmission inspection to be missed.

### Combat and Response
When a crossbeam of the Sangam remnant tower sounds a low tone in the wind, several families are already using that tone as roost coordinates. Move the lamp to a low arm at Nanji and switch off the Sangam side, and the coordinates split in one night. If the insect lamp cannot be moved toward Nanji, a film of droppings and diving birds close the transmission inspection hatch beneath the remnant tower in the same week.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
The record of nonbreeding use of the remnant tower carries into the next month until one side declares its demolition. Recognizing G02-SC2's insect-lamp relocation as a Nanji base opens the Sangam inspection hatch, but leaves that base bearing the cycle of droppings for another month. Choosing demolition leaves the factory-roof shift to bear all of that month's nighttime maintenance.

### Scenario Connections
G02-SC2 notes that choosing to move the lamp to a disused steel tower can shift the Sangam crossbeam tone to a Nanji base. G02-SC1's work noise overlaps the crossbeam's low tone and corrupts the coordinates; G02-SC3's sea wind briefly echoes the same low tone through the bridge cables.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/6/bestiar.en: Bridge Cylinder 'Inspection Hollow' is a fortress formed when the sea wind fills a cylinder of air above the transmission inspection hatch. Wings within the cylinder divide up altitude without direction, determining who can cross without an umbrella.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/6/prose.en:
### Role and Body
When the column of air above the transmitter inspection hatch fills with sea wind, that space becomes a fortress that divides pedestrian traffic. The wings within the circle divide themselves by altitude without direction; anyone crossing without an umbrella meets beaks and flashlight beams along the same line, and a bag strap is torn.

### Origin
As the bridge cables and the air above the inspection hatch became a shared roost for several families, an imaginary fortress arose: a circle that physically blocks the line of people. Field experience showed that a straight push through drove the flock into the alley, so umbrella processions and an alternate staircase were adopted in response.

### Habitat
The circle grows dense only during the day, when the inspection-hatch cover is open; when the cover closes, the birds descend to the bridge’s lower chord. Above the school passage, the circle cannot form and passes through only as a thin band. Above the evacuation stairs, its radius shrinks by the width of the railing.

### Needs and Costs
Maintaining the fortress requires sea wind, an open cover, and an agreement not to aim flashlights into the circle. If a flashlight is pointed at its center, beaks follow the light downward and tear at the bags of those at the back of the line. If the lights are switched off, inspection takes twice as long, cutting into transmission time.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
The circle stays dense only while the sea wind blows in one direction; if the wind reverses, the division by altitude collapses within an hour. Afterward, droppings left on the alternate staircase’s handrail create a slipping hazard for the next evacuation group.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
Individuals within the circle divide themselves only by altitude, without direction, while the controller redirects only the line of people. Breeding pairs abandon their division of territory by radius inside the circle, and juveniles stay at the lowest altitude, level with people’s bags.

### Escalating Threat
When the circle is thin, it is possible to cross without an umbrella by brushing past its edge. Once sea wind fills it, crossing is blocked except in an umbrella procession. If the alternate staircase is opened too late, the back of the line is trapped beneath the circle.

### Combat and Response
Once sea wind fills the column above the inspection hatch, pedestrians cannot cross it except in an umbrella procession. Connecting the alternate staircase to the railing outside the circle first, then aiming flashlights only toward the lower chord, keeps the beaks from descending after the light. If the alternate staircase is opened too late, beaks within the circle follow the flashlights down and tear the bag straps of those at the back of the line.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
The bridge controller must test the umbrella procession for only two crossings and withdraw it before the third line. Keeping that limit reduces traffic but prevents bag damage, and the wait at the back of G02-SC3 stays within one evacuation cycle. Failing to withdraw it preserves traffic volume, but the wait at the back of G02-SC3 exceeds one evacuation cycle.

### Scenario Connections
G02-SC3 identifies this column as the setting for a choice: manage the circle with umbrellas, negotiate an alternate roost and a new bell, or postpone the inspection itself until after breeding season. The work basket in G02-SC1 overlaps with the bell at the circle’s edge, while the transmission shutdown in G02-SC2 closes the cover and briefly thins the circle.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/7/bestiar.en: The fledgling 'Handrail Test' is a young bird that tests the feel of a school handrail the day after removal. It cannot follow a breeding pair yet, and its diving call is still short.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/7/prose.en:
### Role and Body
The day after forced removal, a short-winged juvenile perches on a school handrail and tests its feel. Its diving call is still short, closer to curiosity than a threat. If the testing continues for more than a week, that handrail becomes the new center of the route to school, and nearby classes detour via the stairs.

### Origin
The fiction of a juvenile testing the school route after removal rests on a rule: repeated safety signals and food rewards determine where birds return more than nesting success does. Once the helmets and sticks were gone, the warmth of the handrail remained as the first reward, fixing the fledgling’s place there.

### Habitat
It appears on the handrail only during the morning trip to school and hides behind the playground’s wire fence when the class bell rings. It is not yet heavy enough to stay long at the adults’ places on the factory roof and at the railway crossing. During sea-wind week, it uses a low cable on the bridge railing as a second place to test.

### Needs and Costs
To draw its testing away from the handrail, a decoy roost and an insect lamp must already be in place on the playground tower. Without the decoy, droppings accumulate on the handrail and the health officer on duty is pulled from the morning assignment. Moving the decoy every day makes the fledgling cross the middle of the school route to follow it.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
Its short wings learn to glide in two weeks. Chasing it off the handrail before then moves its testing place to the evacuation-stair handrail. If its feathers are injured, it rests by the drain beside the school infirmary, and the smell sends the younger pupils’ line around the back of the building the next day.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
The fledgling cannot follow a breeding pair; it only tests the handrail’s feel. Its auxiliary warning call is also too short for adults to interpret. Those supervising the school route count its visits to distinguish a test that is becoming established from one that is passing.

### Escalating Threat
On the first day, it perches for only a few seconds. If droppings accumulate on the same handrail by the third day, detours begin. Without a decoy roost, the following week’s route to school is redrawn around that handrail.

### Combat and Response
When the juvenile begins testing the school handrail the day after forced removal, its diving call is still short. Fastening an insect lamp and a rough stick to the playground tower from dawn draws its trial perches that way. If the decoy roost is not placed on the playground tower first, the same handrail becomes the new center of the following week’s route to school.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Until the first injury after removal, the school and Haeryun can leave the space above the handrail as a temporary roost. Doing so keeps pressure from the bridge in G02-SC3 from spilling as much toward the school, but the younger pupils’ line takes the route beneath the wall. Once a child is scratched, that window closes, and the detour stairs cost nearby classes an extra ten minutes every day.

### Scenario Connections
The juvenile testing left by the wholesale nest removal in G02-SC3 begins at this handrail. The horn in G02-SC1 is not yet tied to the fledgling’s expectation of food. If the relocation of the insect lamp in G02-SC2 coincides with the playground decoy, the testing place shifts outside the school.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/8/display.en: Radio Crow Elder Vocal Type 'Startup Sound'

/monster_contents/M003/entries/8/bestiar.en: The elder vocal type 'Startup Sound' stiffens its throat only at the sound of a transformer starting and keeps its wings folded even at a real fire alarm. It cannot lead the flock, and its silence worsens misclassification.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/8/prose.en:
### Role and Body
Beside an old transformer, an elderly bird whose throat stiffens only at the startup sound remains on an insulator with its wings folded even when a real fire alarm rings. This body bears the cost of specialization in a familiar sound pattern: a slower response to unfamiliar alarms. The flock does not scatter until short-circuit smoke has obscured the roof.

### Origin
It is a remnant of the time when birds learned to associate an arrangement of three horn blasts, two inspection-bell rings, and the transformer’s startup sound with food and danger. Imitation at the shared roost passed new sound patterns to younger birds, but this elder’s syrinx could not adapt. That delay became its fictional impairment.

### Habitat
By day it stays on an insulator inside the transformer fence. Even when the night insect lamp comes on, it chooses its perch by following the startup sound rather than the light. It almost never appears at the bridge or school passage, descending to a vent on the factory roof only during a week of power outages when the startup sound has ceased.

### Needs and Costs
To keep this bird from delaying the flock’s dispersal, a three-day course of training with a new low tone must be paired with a change to the alley’s practice of using crow calls as intrusion alarms. Training alone reduces control-system errors but leaves the alley’s cheap surveillance in place. Removing only the practice reduces errors but also silences the ears that used to give early warning of intruders.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
The syrinx loses a note of flexibility each season, taking its lower voice further from the new alarm bell. Dust bathing maintains its feathers, but its auditory learning does not recover. Drying an injured wing with the transformer’s heat makes that warmth yet another false safety signal.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
The elderly bird cannot lead the flock; its silence instead increases mistaken judgments. Even if younger birds take flight at the alarm, this bird’s continued perch causes H02’s classification to remain at 'sign of an impending outage,' and human operators are apt to use that classification as grounds to stop work.

### Escalating Threat
If its wings stay folded through one alarm, misclassification begins. Without the three-day training, the flock disperses only once smoke becomes visible. That delay creates a gap in both transmission and alley intrusion detection.

### Combat and Response
The elderly bird, attuned only to the transformer’s startup sound, remains on an insulator with its wings folded even when a real fire alarm rings. Briefly playing a different low tone outside the fence at dawn for three days delays the folding of its wings by a beat. If it does not hear the new low tone for three days, short-circuit smoke obscures the roof first, and only then does the flock scatter.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
The night-shift worker bears the decision, without a signature, on whether to remove the alley residents’ practice of using crow calls as intrusion alarms from the control network. If it remains, G02-SC2’s misclassification stops both the factory and the railway; reversing that decision within 48 hours permits one more malfunction. Removing it reduces malfunctions, but the cheap surveillance maintained by G02-SC2 disappears from the alley.

### Scenario Connections
G02-SC2 completes its false outage where the machine classification that elevates calls to a sign of an impending outage overlaps with the elderly bird’s silence. The horn sequence in G02-SC1 is the sound pattern this syrinx is slowest to forget. Without three days of training, the new inspection bell in G02-SC3 cannot reach this bird.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/9/bestiar.en: The coexistence roost 'Flag Altitude' is a gesture that divides altitude from the umbrella line only while the flag is on the railing during sea-wind week. Forcing an inspection after the flag comes down destroys that division.

/monster_contents/M003/entries/9/prose.en:
### Role and Body
Only while the flag is raised on the railing during sea-wind week do the gestures of birds at the designated roost separate their altitude from the umbrella line. Forcing an inspection after the flag comes down destroys that division, causing a transmission fault and a pedestrian injury on the same afternoon. Pushing all the nests away at once makes children the substitute targets of attack.

### Origin
The temporary flag recognizing shared use of a roost during XT02 sea-wind week became a gesture of coexistence, joining a negotiating device to a choice to redistribute signals rather than remove the birds entirely. A local agreement to let humans and birds use the same infrastructure without wrecking each other’s warning systems was bound to this flag.

### Habitat
Only the flagged railing and the twenty meters of altitude above it are space for the division; the gesture does not appear on the factory roof, where there is no flag. Breeding pairs’ territorial radii and fledglings’ post-removal handrail tests avoid this space. It overlaps with the umbrella line only when the inspection-hatch column is dense.

### Needs and Costs
To maintain the division, maintenance hours, the section kept in place, and relocation poles must be recorded together in one ledger. If any entry is missing, it cannot be filled again until the next season. During that gap, transmission time bears a season’s risk of failure, or children cross the circle without umbrellas.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
If sea wind tears the flag, failing to replace it that day causes the altitude division to collapse in the morning. The work of moving nests one arm’s length at a time with relocation poles is permitted only after the young have fledged; moving them earlier sends fledglings spilling toward the school handrail.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
The coexistence birds have no leader; they respond to the flag and the ledger entries. Even the mixed calls of the core are answered beneath the flag only at intervals matching the umbrella line. The controller consults missing ledger entries to decide when to lower the flag.

### Escalating Threat
While the flag is up in the morning, altitudes remain divided and there are no injuries. Lowering only the flag in the afternoon and pushing the inspection through collapses the division. Pushing all the nests away to open the bridge immediately leaves a season-long transmission gap and diving attacks directed at children.

### Combat and Response
While the flag is raised on the railing during sea-wind week, birds at the designated roost divide their altitude from the umbrella line. Recording maintenance hours in the same ledger as the flag and opening the inspection hatch only in the morning keeps beaks and flashlight beams from lining up. Forcing an inspection even after the flag comes down destroys the coexistence altitude division, bringing a transmission fault and a pedestrian injury together on the same afternoon.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
A single ledger mediated by Haeryun binds maintenance hours, the section kept in place, and relocation poles together. Any missing entry must wait until the next season to be filled. Choosing immediate availability in G02-SC3 empties all three entries at once, and children’s passage and transmission time pay the price in the same season. The cost of pushing all the nests away to open the bridge immediately is a season-long transmission gap and substitute attacks on children.

### Scenario Connections
G02-SC3 notes that coexistence is delayed a season unless its three options—an umbrella procession, an alternate roost, and an inspection after breeding season—are bound together in this flag ledger. Abandoning the horn in G02-SC1 requires rewriting the ledger’s maintenance hours, while relocating the insect lamp in G02-SC2 trades the section kept in place for the Nanji base.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/0/bestiar.en: Bridge Convergence 'Synchronized Circle' is a scenario phase in which the perches of several families join into one circle. No commander has appeared; it is a convergence of sound patterns on an evening when sea winds and breeding overlap.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/0/prose.en:
### Role and Body
A scenario boss, this convergence gathers the perches of several families into one circle above the Han River bridge cables and transmission inspection hatches. Its flight feathers mimic three horn blasts and two inspection-bell strikes at once, and its eyes distinguish helmets, poles, flashlight reflections, and the angles of umbrellas. It can only connect sparks and transformer sounds to clues about insects and workers; it cannot read the content of transmissions or tell whether a short circuit lies beyond an insulator.

### Origin
During a season when sea winds and the breeding period overlapped in XT02, the West Sea Granary Theater, sound patterns learned separately at the Sangam transmission tower and the Yongsan overhead wires mixed above the bridge, forming this circle. The communal perch of G02-SC3 is the model for its shape, and the young birds' practice of establishing trial perches along school routes after forced removal expanded its radius.

### Habitat
Its central area is the airspace between the overhead-wire junction at the Wangsimni United Line Succession State and the Han River bridge inspection hatch. By day, its members scatter across the factory roofs of the Yeongdeungpo Line Standards Alliance for waste heat, gathering into a ring only on evenings when the sea wind strengthens. When a wire-repair basket rises, some follow its path.

### Needs and Economy
It eats nocturnal insects, leftover protein from markets, and small carcasses; its nests contain stripped fine wire and scraps of fiber. If HC02, the Sinjeong Wheel Guild, frequently replaces the covering and materials grow scarce, the birds tear at railing signs and umbrella handles, increasing territorial attacks. If the covering is neglected, droppings coat the insulators and reduce transmission uptime.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
In spring, breeding pairs each guard an arc of the circle; outside the breeding season, several families converge. When sea winds damage their feathers, their mimicked sounds split and false alarms increase. In the year after a removal, the circle gathers more quickly at the sound of the same inspection bell alone.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
Breeding pairs divide nest defense and food transport between them, but the converged circle has no commander. The Synchronized Circle is a temporary center that shares only sound patterns. Even if H02 Seorin records the order of calls and flight directions, an HC02 human controller decides whether work stops. If one breeding bird disappears, neighboring pairs test the vacant perch, increasing clashes.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, scouts imitate horns and inspection bells from transmission towers and railings, bringing the sound patterns back to the circle. In stage 2, feeding signals and safety warnings become mixed, setting off a chain of dives at workers, detours around school routes, and transmission shutdowns. In stage 3, three false alarms accumulate at the same inspection hatch, and the flock moves in unison at a single signal.

### Combat and Response
Nets, gunfire, and aerial pursuit drive the flock into residential alleys and make it distrust every warning sound pattern. Visual screens, processions of umbrellas, and alternate stairways can redirect its movement; moving insect-attracting lights and the inspection bell to another transmission tower splits the signals it has learned. Success is measured not in carcasses but in fewer short circuits, zero pedestrian injuries, transmission uptime, and the false-alarm rate.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Clearing every nest at once to reopen the bridge immediately removes insect predation and residents' warnings, making walking children and evacuees alternative targets for dives. If HC02 puts repair hours, school and evacuation detours, nest-retention sections, relocation poles, and temporary perches for sea-wind weeks into one ledger, people can share the same infrastructure while accepting the confusion of relearning. Delaying transmission inspection until after the breeding season reduces clashes, but people bear a season of breakdown risk.

### Scenario Connection
The new signal above the bridge in G02-SC3 is the setting for this converged circle; the three horn blasts of G02-SC1 and the diving call of G02-SC2 overlap here as one sound pattern.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/1/bestiar.en: Sea-Wind Variant 'Shore-Feather Perch' is a waterside branch that remembers the breakwater bell and lighthouse first. It does not imitate inland horn sequences, and its space does not overlap with the bridge circle even on the same evening.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/1/prose.en:
### Role and Body
A regional variant, this sea-wind-adapted bird weaves fiber and net scraps into nests on abandoned transmission towers and breakwater railings along the western waterfront. Salt has worn the edges of its beak, so it chooses wet fiber over fine wire; its eyes read bands of insects carried by the sea wind and reflections from the breakwater lighthouse. It remembers waves and the breakwater bell before inland horn sequences, and knows neither the content of transmissions nor the condition of insulators on a distant bridge.

### Origin
It branched off when some birds temporarily moved to the western waterfront outside the breeding season, following the sea winds and insect density coming from the XT02 direction. After young birds displaced from city transmission towers used an abandoned tower on the Nanji shore as a trial perch, the breakwater bell became a feeding reward and changed where they returned the next year.

### Habitat
Only during dry seasons and sea-wind weeks does it leave the Yeongdeungpo Line factory roofs to stay on abandoned towers and breakwater railings along the western waterfront. During the breeding season, it guards its shore perch instead of returning to the bridge ring, so its space does not overlap with the inland converged circle even on the same evening.

### Needs and Economy
It eats insects blown in by the sea wind and leftovers from waterfront markets; its nesting materials are net fragments and wet fiber. Cutting off inland wire covering does not reduce this variant. Moving insect-attracting lights to an abandoned tower makes that tower a new feeding ground and base.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
When sea winds become less frequent, it leaves the shore perch and returns to the factory roofs, but a breakwater bell repeated for a season delays its return. Unless its salt-coated feathers are rinsed with fresh water, its mimicked sounds split; after forced removal, it tests a new perch on the awning of a neighboring fish stall.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
There is no commander at the shore perch either; the birds share only sound patterns. They do not imitate the inland breeding pairs' horns. Even if H02 flags a diving call as a sign of an impending power outage, a person distinguishes it again when the field marker is the breakwater lighthouse. HC02 control decides only whether waterfront work stops and does not count the bridge circle as part of this variant.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, it memorizes the breakwater bell and the lighthouse's flashes as feeding signals. In stage 2, it follows insect-attracting lights to an abandoned tower and swarms over a waterfront inspection basket. In stage 3, during a sea-wind week with no flags, trial perches spread as far as fish-stall awnings, and it targets coastal pedestrians without school-route umbrellas for dives.

### Combat and Response
An umbrella procession designed for inland use folds in the coastal wind and is ineffective, while drone pursuit drives the variant into fish-market alleys. Turning off the insect-attracting lights and changing the breakwater bell to a rhythm distinct from the inspection bell disrupts its learning for several days. It is safer to screen only the basket with net-free visual-blocking cloth. Success indicators are waterfront short circuits, coastal pedestrian injuries, and the false-alarm rate.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Leaving insect-attracting lights at the abandoned shore tower protects inland school routes but makes waterfront workers and the fish market bear the cost of the new base. Returning the lighthouse to a city transmission tower makes school railings trial perches again. Putting temporary flags only on the breakwater during sea-wind weeks and using relocation poles to move only the net nests delays transmission restoration without trading away children's passage and coastal livelihoods on the same evening.

### Scenario Connection
The relocation of insect-attracting lights in G02-SC2 creates this variant's base; the sea-wind week of G02-SC3 enlarges its shore perch; and the abandonment of horns in G02-SC1 leaves the breakwater bell as a new feeding clock.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/2/display.en: Stray Dog Iron Company Leading Adult 'Ironstep'

/monster_contents/M004/entries/2/bestiar.en: The leading adult 'Ironstep' is the longest-lived medium-sized adult and merely proposes movement first. It has no authority to command; the two adults beside it accept or reject its proposal.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/2/prose.en:
### Role and Body
A controller, it is the medium-sized adult that has survived the longest. Its rusty collar ring makes a metallic clinking sound with every step, and its nose distinguishes human scent, disinfectant, and the smell of frozen food thawing. It has no authority to command and merely proposes movement first. H03 Ido can read its passive collar tag only from within about 2 meters, and often misses it because of wet fur and the metal ring.

### Origin
After the collapse, this dog moved between a closed private shelter and a construction-site guard post before joining other wandering families in the vacant lot by the outer wall of the Yongsan Line Yangjae Machineworks Company. As its metallic clinking became a signal that gathered companions, people began calling this gait a leader, but it was never chosen as a pack leader.

### Habitat
By day, it rests in the closed security passage of the Yongsan Line and beneath an overpass. When unloading leftovers increase, it descends to the edge of the nocturnal unloading yard at the Noryangjin Line Charter Transcription State. On nights when XT03 logistics vibrations intensify, its proposed route extends as far as the freezer entrance.

### Needs and Economy
Protein leftovers, discarded meal packs, and filtered water in sealed containers determine the group's density. If HC03, the Magok Life Guild, seals discarded protein too tightly, this dog proposes a detour through market alleys; if it seals it loosely, crowding builds at the unloading yard and contact with people increases.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
When feeding is stable, it proposes defending territory before breeding. If forced capture scatters the group, they gather again where identification tags remain. When its ring breaks, the metallic clinking disappears and regrouping is delayed, so wrapping a broken ring with wire is survival maintenance, not decoration.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
The two adults beside it accept or reject its proposals, while families with pups maintain a separate protected area. Even if H03 reports them together as an aggressive cluster, HC03 mediators separate them again by each dog's identification tag, scent, and companions. If the leading dog falls silent, the families merely return to their last sleeping places; they do not wait for a new order.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, it responds only to specific identification tags and feeding trucks, guarding the edge of the vacant lot. In stage 2, a familiar engine sound and unloading leftovers draw several families into one passage, where they begin following an escort cart. In stage 3, after feeding stops or deceptive capture, the families simultaneously occupy markets and transfer stairs.

### Combat and Response
Direct gunfire and indiscriminate capture merely drive families out of their familiar living areas. Barrier fences, alternate feeding sites, noise reduction, and flags marking pup areas come first; capture is limited to injured dogs or dogs that actually led attacks. Success means zero civilian bites, fewer minutes of unloading delay, and the proportion of families reunited.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Delaying unloading until shelter-code checks are complete reduces misidentification but lets food thaw. Registering current companions and pup care first stabilizes the group, but conflicts with later return claims by former owners. Removing only the leading dog on the pretext of its abandonment history leaves not 48 hours but days of scattered occupation, and closes the civilian reporting network.

### Scenario Connection
The incomplete reading of the rusty name tag in G03-SC1 overlaps with this dog's proposal; the engine sound of G03-SC2 and the freezer encirclement of G03-SC3 occur after the proposal is rejected.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/3/display.en: Stray Dog Iron Company Wanderer 'Empty Ring'

/monster_contents/M004/entries/3/bestiar.en: The wanderer 'Empty Ring' is a lone dog with an empty collar that has been unable to join any family. It does not follow the leader's proposals and is often omitted from the ledger because it has no tag reading.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/3/prose.en:
### Role and Body
An ordinary ecological type, it is a solitary wanderer whose collar ring is empty and makes almost no metallic clinking. It uses its sense of smell to seek the scent of an old feeding station and its hearing to gauge potential companions by the clatter of others' identification tags. Its tag is missing or broken, so H03's short-range readings often show a blank.

### Origin
Separated from people during a crowd evacuation, it moved between vacant lots and drains without joining any family. The empty ring is not decoration but a record of failed reunion.

### Habitat
It roams alone along the edge of the Yongsan Line outer-wall vacant lot and the drain behind the market, approaching the Noryangjin Line entrance only on nights with abundant unloading leftovers. When daytime crowds are dense, it stays motionless in the shade beneath the overpass.

### Needs and Economy
A few scraps from a meal pack and a sip of water from a sealed supply are enough to get it through a day. When protein is sealed away, it descends toward leftovers along children's routes. In areas without both shade and water, it stops moving.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
It does not breed before finding a small family by scent and metallic clinking. If forced into a cage, it refuses food; after release, it avoids the same feeding truck.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It does not follow the leading adult's proposals, checking scents only from a distance. It approaches the sound of an identification tag, then immediately withdraws if an engine sound coincides with an unfamiliar person's gesture. The blank in H03's log is a sign not to treat this dog as nonexistent.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, it leaves only footprints at the edge of the vacant lot. In stage 2, it follows cart wheels at the unloading entrance, causing passersby to hesitate. In stage 3, after deceptive capture, it sits alone on the transfer stairs, not to threaten passage but because it is following leftovers in the children's alley.

### Combat and Response
An individual capture net merely drives it into the market. If an alternate feeding dish is placed toward the vacant lot and people stop moving, it breaks off its approach on its own. Luring it by filling the empty ring with a fake piece of metal means it will not come even when called for rescue later.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Tying the lone dog to a feeding cart to incorporate it into an existing family fills a numerical ledger but creates a false kinship and reduces space for pups. Leaving it to wander increases market intrusions, but avoids a return dispute if its former owner appears. The moment a tagless dog is entered in the punishment ledger, the window for negotiation closes.

### Scenario Connection
This dog is the unreadable fourth blank in G03-SC1, and the engine sound in G03-SC2 draws the wanderer toward the unloading route, making its movement look like a family reunion.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/4/display.en: Stray Dog Iron Company Unloading Feeder 'Offal Nose'

/monster_contents/M004/entries/4/bestiar.en: The unloading feeder 'Offal Nose' feeds at the entrance, its nose fixed on thawing drips and fish offal. It rejects the vacant-lot leader's proposal and guards only the unloading corridor.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/4/prose.en:
### Role and Body
An ordinary ecological type, it is an unloading-area feeder whose nose is fixed on fish offal and the smell of frozen food thawing. Its paw pads have adapted to floors wet with melted ice, so it favors only slippery unloading yards, and its collar fragment is short, making its metallic clinking faint. It follows the intensity of the thawing smell before human gestures.

### Origin
Once the stream of leftovers from nocturnal unloading on the Noryangjin Line became reliable, it split from the vacant-lot family and made the unloading-yard entrance its sleeping place. Its guard-dog lineage retains the habit of waiting at night, but it has no duty to guard people.

### Habitat
Its core territory is the Noryangjin Line corridor of fishery and frozen-food leftovers and the unloading-yard shade. By day, it withdraws to a drain; when XT03 logistics vibrations intensify, it pushes its nose as far as the lip of the freezer entrance.

### Needs and Economy
Its main resources are fish offal and thawing drips. If sealing is tightened, it immediately slips into market alleys. Without a sealed water supply, it drinks thaw water directly, keeping its population concentrated in one place.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
The more regular the unloading schedule, the more territorial urine accumulates at the entrance, but breeding does not increase. If unloading moves to another freezer, its nose follows the new drips within three days, moving its sleeping place.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It rejects the leading adult's proposal to go to the vacant lot and guards only the unloading corridor. It feeds loosely alongside only two or three dogs drawn by the same offal smell, and does not enter the territory of families with pups. Even if H03 counts them together as an unloading-yard cluster, a mediator separates them again by their paths along the thawing smell.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, it scavenges offal only after unloading ends. In stage 2, it blocks the entrance before carts stop, adding minutes to unloading. In stage 3, on a night when feeding has stopped, it surrounds the freezer lip, overlapping with merchants' passage.

### Combat and Response
Turning unloading-yard disinfection into poisoned bait lets carcasses spoil the water quality and drives the surviving dogs into alleys. Putting leftovers in sealed bins, moving them to an alternate feeding dish in the vacant lot, and reducing noise only at the entrance restores spacing between carts. Success means fewer minutes of unloading delay and zero bites.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Sealing discarded protein more tightly cleans the unloading yard but makes children's routes an alternative feeding ground. Moving nocturnal unloading to another freezer preserves this dog's learned pattern but raises transport and refrigeration costs for Noryangjin Line merchants. Using an offal dish as a capture lure means its nose will no longer respond even to regular feeding.

### Scenario Connection
When the engine sound in G03-SC2 gathers families on the unloading route, this dog takes the entrance first. The offal corridor becomes the point of contention in the freezer encirclement of G03-SC3.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/5/display.en: Stray Dog Iron Company Daytime Hider 'Drain Shade'

/monster_contents/M004/entries/5/bestiar.en: The daytime hider 'Drain Shade' stays in drains and beneath overpasses to avoid daytime crowds. While daylight remains, it does not move even if the leader heads for the vacant lot.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/5/prose.en:
### Role and Body
An ordinary ecological type, it hides in drains and beneath overpasses to avoid daytime crowds. It senses differences in shade temperature and lingering disinfectant odors more than it relies on sight, and moves between pipe entrances on short legs. Its metal fragment is wrapped in tape to keep it from striking the pipe wall, so it makes almost no sound during the day.

### Origin
When the crowded daytime market took over the vacant lot, dogs outside the unloading families learned to sleep in the shade of drains and overpasses. The tape is not a sign that a person wrapped it; it consists of fiber remnants the dog rubbed on itself to avoid being startled by pipe noise.

### Habitat
Drains and the shade beneath overpasses between the Yongsan Line vacant lot and the Noryangjin Line market form its daytime territory. Only at night does it join the unloading corridor; if the shade is removed, it is driven beneath the transfer stairs.

### Needs and Economy
Shade and a sealed water supply that has not been recontaminated set the upper limit on its population density. When resting space is scarcer than food, it lies down on daytime pedestrian routes.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
If the tape comes loose, pipe vibrations startle it into abandoning the shade and emerging onto the stairs. If a forced search clears the drain, hiding places re-form on the transfer stairs that same evening.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It does not move while daylight remains, even if the leader proposes going to the vacant lot. It shares shade with families with pups at different times, but their feeding turns do not overlap. Even when H03's daytime log is blank, a person must check for a heat source in the shade with a flashlight.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, only footprints remain at the drain entrance. In stage 2, it comes into sight of daytime pedestrians beneath the overpass. In stage 3, after the shade is removed, it occupies the transfer stairs even by day.

### Combat and Response
High-pressure washing and toxic smoke drive the dogs into alleys and increase bites. Opening an alternative shade canopy and a sealed water container toward the vacant lot, while only partially blocking the drain, restores daytime passage. Success is measured by daytime encounter distance and hours of stair occupation.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Keeping the space beneath the overpass lit at all times clears it for public safety but moves the hiders to the transfer stairs. Leaving shade and recognizing the animals' need to rest by day could let a theft ring use their gathering time to identify gaps in warehouse security, so location records must be shared with a delay. Treating daytime hiders as targets for extermination destroys both animal-protection ethics and the reporting network.

### Scenario Connection
When the reading at the edge of the unloading yard in G03-SC1 conflicts with the daytime blank, this shade is a possible cause. Stair occupation in G03-SC3 is the price of removing that shade.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/6/display.en: Stray Dog Iron Company Reunion Worker 'Metal-Shard Cry'

/monster_contents/M004/entries/6/bestiar.en: The reunion worker 'Metal-Shard Cry' performs the signaling work of wearing identification-tag fragments to call scattered companions. It gives no orders, and duplicate readings can easily leave one dog recorded under two codes.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/6/prose.en:
### Role and Body
A specialist that hangs leash rings and pieces of identification tags across its body, using the sound of metal scraps as a signal to reunite. Its hearing distinguishes the rhythm of metal impacts more finely than engine noise, while its sense of smell matches companions' scents to the sounds. With several tags on one body, H03 can easily read it twice under two codes.

### Origin
After forced capture scattered families, they gathered again around individuals whose tags remained; that habit became concentrated in this body. Adding metal scraps is not decoration but the work of marking a dispersed reunion network.

### Habitat
It moves between vacant lots and loading yards, choosing places beneath concrete walls that reflect sound well. It seldom stays on dirt or flooded ground, where its signal fades.

### Needs and Economy
Fallen tag fragments and wire, more than food, sustain its specialty. Confiscating the markings delays family reunions and increases simultaneous appearances in markets and stairways.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
When a ring rusts and its sound dulls, it picks up and hangs a new metal scrap. If duplicate readings continue for three days, the ledger counts this one body as 'two dogs' until a mediator compares their appearances.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It moves later than a leading adult but calls scattered companions with sound and rejoins small families. It gives no orders, only marks a signal. It quiets the sound near pups.

### Escalating Threat
At Stage 1 it calls only companions with short metal scraps in a vacant lot. At Stage 2 it amplifies echoes in the loading passage and gathers several families into one line. At Stage 3, after a deceptive lure exploits the sound, it ignores every rhythm resembling a rescue call.

### Combat and Response
Recording the metal sound as bait makes short-term capture easy but destroys trust in all subsequent rescue signals. Sound-absorbing cloth beneath the wall and an alternative feeding dish reduce only the echoes, allowing reunions to return to the vacant lot. Success is measured by the family reunion rate and fewer false calls.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Using surviving tag data solely to find missing families means accepting duplicate readings without creating a punishment ledger. Cutting away every metal scrap buys quiet but collapses the reunion network and increases occupation of stairways. The cost of gathering them with a false rescue signal is silence when someone is truly hurt.

### Scenario Links
The three distinct shelter codes in G03-SC1 may be duplicate readings of one body, and the dispersed reunion network of G03-SC3 rests on these metal markers.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/7/display.en: Abandoned-Dog Iron Pack Feeding Memory 'Idling Ear'

/monster_contents/M004/entries/7/bestiar.en: Feeding Memory 'Idling Ear' remembers the engine sound of a particular feeding truck as a safety signal. On hearing it idle, it puts the vehicle ahead of the leader's proposal and draws its family to the loading route.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/7/prose.en:
### Role and Body
A specialist that remembers the idling engine and wheel sounds of a particular feeding truck as a safe human signal. Its hearing distinguishes the idling rhythm from an unfamiliar engine, and it relaxes its guard only when it also smells the original driver's scent. A hand gesture alone will not bring it near.

### Origin
After the feeding truck on the closed security passage stopped coming, reproducing the same idle still drew scattered families to the loading route; that learning remained in its body. The social learning of G03-SC2 was the model for this specialty.

### Habitat
It appears between the Yongsan Line security-passage entrance and the Noryangjin Line loading route only at night when engine noise is audible. It stops one circuit away from a mobile feeding station without an engine.

### Needs and Economy
The familiar idle, more than a food pack, is its condition for approaching. If the vehicle changes, it refuses food for several days and relies more on loading-yard leftovers.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
When the original driver disappears, aggression and refusal of food both rise. Learning a new driver's scent alongside the feeding procedure takes several days, during which the loading volume must be reduced.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It gives the vehicle priority over the leading adult. When it hears the idle, it pulls its family toward the loading route and temporarily overrides the leader's proposal. Even if H03 records this as group movement, the mediator separates them by vehicle.

### Escalating Threat
At Stage 1 it merely pricks up its ears outside the old passage. At Stage 2, when the idle is reproduced, it draws several families to the cart. At Stage 3, after engine noise is used in deceptive capture, it treats every approaching vehicle as hostile.

### Combat and Response
Using engine noise to lure it into a cage opens the passage immediately but spends trust like a disposable resource. Placing an engine-free mobile feeding station somewhere new each day preserves the signal but costs labor and refrigeration. Success is measured by the speed of restored loading, the days needed to relearn, and zero bites.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Depending on the original driver alone clears the passage at once, but that person's absence collapses the entire agreement. Gradual familiarity with a new driver makes people bear several days of lost distribution. Deceiving its trust to buy quick safety also makes rescue workers into enemies later.

### Scenario Links
The pack that remembers the feeding truck in G03-SC2 is this specialist's setting; if feeding stops as well in G03-SC3, the night without an idling engine becomes a siege.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/8/display.en: Abandoned-Dog Iron Pack Nursery Specialist 'Pup Shield'

/monster_contents/M004/entries/8/bestiar.en: Nursery Specialist 'Pup Shield' holds a veto that blocks even the leader's proposal within the pups' area. It is a barrier outside the command structure; if a feeding cart crosses it, pups are left behind.

/monster_contents/M004/entries/8/prose.en:
### Role and Body
