As the first core was repeatedly exposed to disinfection and light, some individuals moved their breeding site to the cooler tray opposite and split off. They left few droppings and only juvenile footprints, breaking the impression that the image showed a single colony mass.

### Habitat
It occupies the cable layer opposite the Gwangjin Line shopping arcade and, when evacuation crowds grow dense, the space behind the Yeouido Line soup kitchen wall. The more crowded the warm core becomes near the bright platform, the more this core clings to a quieter tray.

### Needs and Economy
Small amounts of protein leftovers and weak leaking heat suffice to keep its young warm. If bait still disappears on this side after scraps are cut off from the warm core, the colony's density has shifted, not vanished.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
If individuals crowd in on the night the warm core disappears, the opposite core grows into a temporary center. Only after seven nights without new juvenile tracks is this core considered dormant.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
No leader is replaced; only the traces move. If H05 tracks only the large heat spot, it misses this core's flow and the movement spreading to surviving nests immediately after one site is removed.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, thermal imaging that shows only the warm core conflicts with juvenile tracks on the opposite side. In stage 2, movement concentrates at this core after the warm core is sealed. In stage 3, removing only the first nest without a survey shifts the center to this tray and the stairwell cables.

### Combat and Response
Covering the opposite core with poison kills non-target young and other wildlife first. Do not block this tray before checking every core, testing only an escape route in one section, or obtaining a heat map.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Buying HP09 Digital Media City Trust House's old cable heat map shortens the survey but requires handing over past passage records. Surveying every core on foot preserves privacy but delays opening the passage; ignoring the unseen core divides those who want immediate sanitation from those seeking to prevent mistaken captures.

### Scenario Connections
This opposite core is the setting of G05-SC1, 'The Second Core Nest.' When the hub is blocked in G05-SC3, the hidden core adds a branch into the unloading passage; the wrongly closed shutter in G05-SC2 sends pressure from the opposite core toward the stairs.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/3/display.en: Transfer Rat Colony Cable Stronghold 'Tray Warmth'

/monster_contents/M008/entries/3/bestiar.en: The cable stronghold 'Tray Warmth' is a form of occupation that uses the cable tray itself as both a travel route and a store of warmth. The damp stretch poses a more extensive threat than any individual's teeth.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/3/prose.en:
### Role and Body
An environmental stronghold: a form of occupation that uses the cable tray itself as both a travel route and a store of warmth. Droppings and moisture damage wire sheathing, and the damp stretch of tray poses a more extensive threat than the teeth of any one individual.

### Origin
When insulated pipes and power cable trays were laid side by side at the transfer connection, the metal route, still warm in winter, became a sleeping place. Each lighting failure raised fears of contagion, but the cause is damaged sheathing and moisture, not a pathogen.

### Habitat
The main-line tray beneath the Gwangjin Line transfer shopping arcade is its center. When evacuation crowds grow dense, branches extend into the Yeouido Line evacuation stairwell cables; frequently disinfected sections are crossed only at night.

### Needs and Economy
Pipe heat and fine food scraps on the tray sustain the stronghold. Reducing scraps while leaving the tray open allows its warmth to remain and its density to rebound.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
Moisture lingers where sheathing is damaged, making that stretch the next sleeping place. This stronghold is considered diminished only when insulation resistance returns to baseline and no reverse-running tracks appear for three days.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
Movement along the tray follows food traces toward the cores; no one directs it. Unless HC05 compares monthly sheathing-damage rates with humidity, it will mistake heat spots alone for the stronghold.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, nighttime crossing tracks extend along the tray. In stage 2, blocking one stretch reroutes movement toward warmth on another tray. In stage 3, dampness reaches the stairwell cables and cuts the time the electronic information boards remain available.

### Combat and Response
Filling the tray with water to drive the rats out causes a short circuit first. Keep it cool and dry and close the lids from the rear forward. Consider predatory birds in the open courtyard only if collision markings and droppings cleanup are in place.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Sealing every tray reduces colony movement, but lighting inspectors must take detours and the electronic information boards may remain off longer. Opening the lids only at night makes inspection easier, but the pathfinders learn to time their openings accordingly.

### Scenario Connections
The reverse movement in G05-SC2 occurs when this tray stronghold connects to the stairwell cables. The opposite tray in G05-SC1 has the same warmth-providing structure, and the hub power outage in G05-SC3 results from sheathing damage spreading as far as the courtyard.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/4/display.en: Transfer Rat Colony Shutter Stronghold 'After-Closing Shade'

/monster_contents/M008/entries/4/bestiar.en: The shutter stronghold 'After-Closing Shade' is an occupation that uses the space behind shop shutters where traffic has ceased as temporary storage. If the soup kitchen shutter is closed first, the individuals in the shade reverse course into the evacuation stairwell.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/4/prose.en:
### Role and Body
An environmental stronghold: an occupation that uses the space behind shop shutters where traffic has ceased as temporary storage and a shaded travel route. Its individuals crouch more compactly than those in the trays and depend on air currents through shutter gaps and crumbs on the floor.

### Origin
Food scraps collected late after closing became lodged in shutter rails, turning the shaded space into storage. The habit of closing the soup kitchen shutter first pushed the rats in that shade toward the stairs.

### Habitat
It occupies the shutter line of the Gwangjin Line transfer shopping arcade and the gaps that open only at night. When evacuees fill the area in front of the shops by day, the rats retreat deeper into the rail grooves.

### Needs and Economy
Its resources are after-closing food scraps and warm air leaking through shutter gaps. Eliminating the nighttime gaps reduces the occupation, but scraps left in the rails revive it within a day.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
Keeping shutters down for long periods lets moisture in the shade rust the rails. Unless the Gwangjin Line measures the weight of food scraps left after closing and delays in collection, the shade becomes an established seasonal stronghold.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
The shade is not a center but a waiting place between cores. When food traces lead back to the warm core, movement drains out of the shade as well.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, droppings accumulate in the after-closing shade. In stage 2, closing the soup kitchen shutter first sends its occupants back toward the Yeouido Line evacuation stairwell. In stage 3, the hub shop shutters also come down, blocking the unloading route.

### Combat and Response
Lowering all the shutters at once leaves only the open emergency stairwell. Adjust the nighttime shutter gaps and close the shops from the rear forward, moving bags of food scraps away from the rails first.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
If HC05 negotiates nighttime shutter gaps, shop work is delayed but the stairwell can be cleared. Closing the soup kitchen first to speed up distribution makes evacuee traffic overlap with movement through the cable layer.

### Scenario Connections
G05-SC2, 'The Sealing-Sequence Error,' pushes the rats in this shade toward the stairs. In G05-SC3, the hub shutters create a barrier to unloading; the escape-route test in G05-SC1 keeps one unoccupied shuttered space closed for a long period to shift the rats in the shade.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/5/display.en: Transfer Rat Colony Juvenile Form 'Young Tracks'

/monster_contents/M008/entries/5/bestiar.en: The juvenile form 'Young Tracks' consists of young still bound to a core and their footprints. The tracks are not evidence of contagion but marks on the floor indicating a hidden core; the young cannot sense distant air currents.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/5/prose.en:
### Role and Body
A life-stage form consisting of young still bound to a core and their footprints. Their whiskers are too short to sense distant air currents, and they tire quickly on brightly lit floors. They are not evidence of contagion but marks on the floor indicating a hidden core.

### Origin
Young born in both the warm and opposite cores were moved first to the cooler tray, leaving tracks. People read the tracks as signs of disease spreading, but the colony spreads no unusual pathogen.

### Habitat
Dry dust in the opposite tray and the lower part of the soup kitchen wall. They cannot reach the heavily disinfected platform; if they do, increased energy expenditure slows their growth.

### Needs and Economy
Crumbs brought by their mothers and a little warmth are enough. Placing bait in front of the young makes capture easier, but afterward the mothers will not approach even during routine collection.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
If several generations endure the bright platform, nocturnal behavior becomes more pronounced, but the breeding rate falls. This is not a sudden mutation but a shift toward those that survived.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
The young receive no orders and follow only their mothers' openings. If H05 sees footprints without a heat spot, it postpones classifying the core as active and records a non-target check first.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, juvenile tracks appear where thermal imaging shows none. In stage 2, disturbing the warm core causes the young to be moved into the shutter shade. In stage 3, mistaken captures scatter the mothers into the stairwell.

### Combat and Response
Capturing everything where young tracks appear as evidence immediately raises non-target deaths. Mark only the sections with tracks and open a one-way escape route; clean those floors after the adults have moved out.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Those seeking immediate sanitation demand disinfection as soon as tracks appear, while those seeking to prevent mistaken captures spend time checking for non-target animals. Whether that time goes to opening the passage or to verification is the cost posed by this juvenile form.

### Scenario Connections
G05-SC1 begins with juvenile tracks in the opposite tray. In G05-SC2, choosing to leave bait deliberately increases scraps in front of the young; the arrival of birds in G05-SC3 exposes them to non-target predation.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/6/display.en: Transfer Rat Colony Aged Form 'Escape-Route Memory'

/monster_contents/M008/entries/6/bestiar.en: The aged form 'Escape-Route Memory' is an old individual whose body has learned the sequence of toxic spraying, ultrasound, and sealing panels. It does not become a leader; it merely shows which way it escapes first.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/6/prose.en:
### Role and Body
An aged life-stage form: an old individual whose body has learned the sequence of toxic spraying, ultrasound, and sealing panels. Its teeth and whiskers have dulled and are used less for foraging than for choosing an open direction. It cannot decipher electronic sounds; it only avoids the intervals between vibrations.

### Origin
In sections where the same pest-control sequence was repeated over several seasons, survivors learned to avoid the dangerous sequence and find an open escape route more quickly. This is learning, not a sudden bodily change; it comes at the cost of greater energy expenditure and reduced breeding.

### Habitat
Rather than the frequently treated Gwangjin Line lower level, it stays in the shade of stairwell cables and unloading thresholds that have been open before. It can endure a cold, bright platform but cannot remain there long.

### Needs and Economy
It can survive a day on few food scraps, but quickly curtails movement when far from a heat source. If the same ultrasound pattern sounds again, it leaves that section even if food is present.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
It contributes little to breeding and leaves only routes behind. Even after an old individual dies, the survivors avoid the sequence it learned; removing the body does not erase that learning.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It does not become a leader; it merely shows which way it escapes first. Younger pathfinders connect the space it leaves behind with openings.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, it escapes ahead of a familiar pest-control sequence. In stage 2, it remembers a sealing layout open in only one direction and draws the group that way. In stage 3, it completes the pattern of closing the soup kitchen first by reversing into the stairwell.

### Combat and Response
Repeating the same poison and ultrasound only makes avoidance faster. Change the sequence, open a one-way escape route toward an area without people, then close it from the rear forward. Do not use flames because of cable sheathing and areas used by children.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Fast, blanket spraying may appear to reduce the old individuals, but it increases exposure for children and companion animals, while survivors learn to retreat into deeper layers. Making the sequence public and rebuilding the process from food-scrap collection takes time, but can keep non-target deaths close to zero.

### Scenario Connections
This aged form embodies the mechanism by which the network connecting the cores remembers the sealing sequence in G05-SC2. Choosing to remove only the first nest in G05-SC1 also shifts the center toward the open side it knows, while opening the courtyard in G05-SC3 introduces a new pattern of predation it has not learned to avoid.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/7/display.en: Transfer Rat Colony Coexistence Form 'Collection Interval'

/monster_contents/M008/entries/7/bestiar.en: The coexistence form 'Collection Interval' remains, at reduced density, only in sections where food scraps are collected on a regular schedule. It emerges only after the collection cart's vibrations have passed; eradication is not a condition.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/7/prose.en:
### Role and Physiology
A coexistence type that remains at low density only in sections where food-waste collection and shutter intervals are regular. It does not communicate with people; when access to food decreases and its path diverges from the evacuation route, it retreats without attacking.

### Origin
As extermination-focused disinfection was repeated, the colony moved deeper into the cables. Once collection sacks passed at the same time each day, some individuals remained that ate only the crumbs left outside that interval. The rhythm of food-distribution labor, not a stigma, shaped this body.

### Habitat
The closed-shop passages of the Gwangjin Line and the outer edge of the Yeouido Line’s food-waste route. During weeks of heavy unloading, it rarely crosses beyond the double-sealed line toward XT05.

### Needs and Economy
Fine scraps left after collection and a little warmth are enough. If collection is postponed to speed up distribution, the interval breaks down and rerouting becomes entrenched.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
If density drops sharply, scraps in the drainage grooves ferment and insects multiply; chemicals and cleaning then increase the burden on food areas instead. Even after the population falls, maintaining coexistence means tracking both the degree of decay and the number of insects caught.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It does not compete for the central core and emerges only after the collection cart’s vibrations have passed. If HC05 records the food-waste cycle, construction sequence, and nighttime intervals in one ledger, its movements shift away from the evacuation passage.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, collection is delayed by a day and the interval widens. In stage 2, the postponed food waste fixes a rerouted path beneath the shutters. In stage 3, only the refugee area is sealed off under the stigma of contagion, pushing the coexistence type deeper and making recovery difficult.

### Combat and Response
Counting captures of the coexistence type as a success only increases collection labor, while the population shifts to another core. Low temperatures, dry conditions, and collection on a fixed schedule are the basics; the passage can be cleared without introducing predatory birds.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Extermination is not a condition. The cost lies in deciding whose passage and cleaning work to delay for safety; if the risk is passed only to refugees, HC05’s mediation ledger will subsequently close. During XT05 unloading weeks, supporting temporary double sealing preserves both food distribution and this interval.

### Scenario Connections
The bait diversion of G05-SC2 and the staggered unloading of G05-SC3 determine whether this interval survives, while the investigative delay in G05-SC1 also interacts with the collection cycle.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/8/display.en: Transfer Rat Colony Hub Boss 'Unloading Barrier'

/monster_contents/M008/entries/8/bestiar.en: The hub boss 'Unloading Barrier' is not a single rat but a high-density movement formed when branches from several cores converge in the concourse after XT05 protein unloading. No leader has appeared.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/8/prose.en:
### Role and Physiology
A scenario boss: not a single rat, but a high-density movement that blocks the transfer hub after XT05 protein unloading. No leader has appeared; branches from several cores simply converge in one concourse when unloading residue coincides with open escape routes. Their whiskers detect the smell of thawing and cart vibrations, but not distant heat spots.

### Origin
During a week when frozen protein from the Incheon Trust Enclave was released all at once, crumbs remained on the hub floor and shop shutters came down simultaneously, forming this barrier. Broadcasts searching for a king of contagion obscured the cause.

### Habitat
The transfer-hub concourse and the area in front of the freight elevator. Normally dispersed between the Warm Core and the Counter-Core, they fill the hub floor only on nights when unloading overlaps.

### Needs and Economy
Unloading drips and carbohydrate crumbs sustain the barrier. Staggered unloading thins it; leaving food waste piled in the hub brings passage to a halt overnight.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
Once unloading ends, the population returns to its cores, but damaged cable sheathing and droppings remain. The barrier is resolved only when there has been no movement against the designated flow for three days, no sign of a new core for seven nights, and transit times have returned to baseline.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
Treating the mass in the hub as a commander concentrates pest control in one place. H05 records heat spots, droppings, and disappearing bait separately, while HC05 publishes electrical shorts, contamination, transit times, and non-target deaths together.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, only crossing tracks increase in the hub on the day after unloading. In stage 2, core closures coincide with unloading, drawing branches into the concourse. In stage 3, the hub is blocked and a proposal to introduce predatory birds is raised.

### Combat and Response
Introducing birds into the concourse may reduce the colony, but it creates collisions, bird droppings, and a need for permanent staffing. Phased escape routes and sealing have fewer side effects but delay distribution; fire burns the hub’s wiring.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Opening a concourse equipped with markers and monitoring merely transfers one ecological problem into another predator–prey relationship; it does not transfer responsibility. Phased sealing delays evacuation. If XT05 staggers its unloading schedule, it avoids creating non-target risks, but the question remains of who bears the higher cost of frozen goods and the food losses.

### Scenario Connections
G05-SC3, 'Predators of the Open Concourse,' is the setting for this unloading barrier; the hidden core of G05-SC1 and the wrongly placed shutter of G05-SC2 are branches that make it grow.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/9/display.en: Transfer Rat Colony Unloading Variant 'Frozen Gap'

/monster_contents/M008/entries/9/bestiar.en: The unloading variant 'Frozen Gap' is an elevator-passage branch that follows thawing drips before shop crumbs. It does not follow the Warm Core’s movements, waiting only for unloading vibrations.

/monster_contents/M008/entries/9/prose.en:
### Role and Physiology
A regional variant adapted to the freight-elevator passage where residue from frozen and deep-sea protein reaches it. Its paws stay on cold metal for long periods, and its nose follows thawing drips before shop crumbs. It uses intermittent unloading vibrations, rather than the heat of the inland Warm Core’s pipes, as the clock for its resting place.

### Origin
During a week of large protein deliveries from the XT05 side, it split from the Warm Core and entered the elevator rail grooves. Cutting off food waste from the shopping area did not reduce this variant; the unloading cycle became its feeding clock.

### Habitat
The freight-elevator passage and the shade beneath its threshold. It seldom descends into the heavily disinfected area below the shops; in weeks without unloading, it stays behind the passage insulation and limits its movements.

### Needs and Economy
Thawing drips and packaging fragments are its main resources. Collecting shop food waste alone does not lower its density, and if the temporary double-sealed line is broken, it spills onto the hub floor.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
Staggered unloading slows breeding, while releasing everything at once causes overcrowding in the passage. Spending long periods on cold metal raises energy use, so it has fewer young than the Warm Core.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It does not follow the Warm Core’s movements, waiting only for elevator vibrations. If H05 clears only the shop heat spots, it misses this variant in the rail grooves.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, droppings increase in the rail grooves on the night after unloading. In stage 2, delayed sealing lets it spill into the hub. In stage 3, after it blocks the hub, a proposal to introduce predators into the concourse lumps this variant together with the rest.

### Combat and Response
Pumping poison gas into the elevator exposes people along the exhaust route first. Stagger unloading, support double sealing first, and move only the drips in the rail grooves into sealed containers.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Concentrating unloading into one night to protect food distribution lets Frozen Gap block the hub and increases pressure to introduce birds. Staggering the schedule avoids non-target predation, but XT05 and the Gwangjin Line must share the food losses and higher logistics costs. If those costs are offset by sealing off refugees, the variant moves into deeper shafts.

### Scenario Connections
The staggered unloading and double sealing of G05-SC3 disrupt this variant’s feeding clock. The bait in G05-SC2 draws drips into the hub, bringing the variant and the Warm Core into the same passage. The core investigation in G05-SC1 leaves a warning not to mistake the rail grooves for a second core.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/0/display.en: Migratory Wetland Predator Group Open-Water Occupant 'Broadwing Perch'

/monster_contents/M009/entries/0/bestiar.en: The open-water occupant 'Broadwing Perch' does not direct the flock with calls; it covers open water first through its size and wingspan. Despite its designation as a controller, it gives no orders.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/0/prose.en:
### Role and Physiology
A controller: an adult waterbird that covers open water first through its size and wingspan, rather than directing the flock with calls. Its eyes distinguish reflections on the water, the colors of work vests, and drone silhouettes; from engine noise and loudspeakers, it can judge only distance. It knows nothing of electronic signals or the water-level numbers inside the sluice gates, and its ankles sink at muddy edges, preventing it from standing there long.

### Origin
When the fragmented Han River–Nanji wetlands dried up and only the water in front of Seoul Station’s central records deck remained, the first waterbird to arrive occupied the open surface, placing this body at the center. The overlapping shallows of G06-SC1 are its stage; the water left after HC06 turned on the pumps for visibility fixed its occupation in place.

### Habitat
By day it spreads its flock across the middle of Seoul Station’s central shallow water; when the level falls, it moves to the Gangnam Line drainage pond. It passes over the bridge walkway but does not stay there, and its talons are unsuited to wire perches.

### Needs and Economy
Aquatic plants and suspended organic matter are its food; safe open water and a short takeoff distance are what it needs to stay. If HC06 lowers the water level, suspended matter gathers in one strip and strengthens its hold. Holding the water level steady increases its numbers and, with them, the risk of train collisions.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
It grows larger only during spring and autumn stopovers; outside the migratory seasons, its wings become lighter and the birds disperse. When its feathers are soaked in turbid water, takeoff is delayed, exposing it to pursuit by raptors. If forcibly dispersed for a season, it occupies the same water earlier at the next stopover.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It gives no orders. When the water surface narrows, shorebirds are merely pushed toward the edges and raptors toward the wires. Even if H06 Park Sol combines them into one score, the HC06 duty officer records altitude and water zones separately. If this bird leaves, the open water is vacated and shorebirds spread as far as the trackside.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, it covers the middle of the narrowed water, blocking the view from the records deck. In stage 2, a single raptor pursuit sends the dense flock surging across the view of the sluice gates and the train arrival and departure tracks. In stage 3, after the same collision occurs three times, the response must set both zone-specific water levels and slowdown times rather than call for extermination.

### Combat and Response
Gunfire and nets scatter the flock to fountains and rooftop water catchments, making its next stopover unpredictable. Zone-specific water levels, fishmeal-waste collection, and drone altitude limits are the basics. Success is measured by the duration of clear sightlines, zero collisions, and turbidity—not carcasses.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Running the pumps longer to expand the open water increases labor and energy use; drying the water merely to gain visibility brings dust, stench, and rodents down on residents. Creating a new shorebird feeding ground outside the depot leaves this bird’s occupation intact while reducing crowding at the edges, but citizens bear the land and dredging costs.

### Scenario Connections
The overlapping water of G06-SC1 is the stage for this occupation; the slowdown learning of G06-SC2 and the takeoffs during the migratory-bird week of G06-SC3 follow in a chain from the same body.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/1/display.en: Migratory Wetland Predator Group Roving Waterbird 'Driftwood'

/monster_contents/M009/entries/1/bestiar.en: The roving waterbird 'Driftwood' is a medium-sized waterbird that follows bands of floating organic matter instead of holding the middle of the water. Even when Broadwing Perch covers the surface, using only the band at the edge avoids conflict.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/1/prose.en:
### Role and Physiology
A common ecological type: a medium-sized waterbird that follows bands of floating organic matter rather than holding the middle of the water. Its bill sorts plant fragments from fishmeal scraps, and its eyes notice oil slicks before the color of rubbish. It cannot understand vibrations in wires or radar classifications, and gives up diving when turbidity prevents it from seeing the bottom.

### Origin
During a season when rain washed fishmeal from market unloading into the edges of Seoul Station’s central water, individuals displaced from the open surface split off and pursued only floating matter. Standing water in the unsuccessfully restored wetland was a feeding ground; the longer collection was delayed, the farther their roaming route extended from the unloading area to the drainage pond.

### Habitat
Ordinarily it circles in the slow current outside the mudline of Seoul Station’s central water. When the wetland dries, it briefly moves to inland park fountains and rooftop water catchments. It visits the Gangnam Line pond only when floating matter gathers there, and does not fly over the train arrival and departure tracks.

### Needs and Economy
It feeds more on floating organic matter and discarded fishmeal than on aquatic plants; a band of scent, not a clean water surface, sustains it. If HC06 collects the waste, it does not go to the pond. If the waste is left, it follows it low into the unloading alleys, overlapping with pedestrians.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
If an oil slick mats its feathers during a stopover season, taking off becomes difficult and it retreats to fountains. After forced dispersal, it searches for the same smell from farther away. When the floating matter is cut off, its numbers fall the following season and it does not join the flock occupying the open water.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
There is neither command nor a spacing rule. It follows floating matter when it moves; even when Broadwing Perch covers the surface, it avoids conflict by using only the band at the edge. If H06 turns its roaming tracks into a single hostility score, HC06 changes only the waste-collection time.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, rain washes fishmeal from unloading into a band beneath the records deck. In stage 2, the band extends to the drainage pond and waterbirds skim the edge of the depot tracks. In stage 3, the smell reaches fountains and rooftops, turning urban water catchments into temporary stopovers.

### Combat and Response
Horns and drones drive it into alley puddles while leaving the band of scent in place. Fishmeal collection and covers at the unloading area break the route. Success is measured by the number of incursions onto depot tracks and by turbidity, not carcasses.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Leaving fishmeal at the market to keep the pond clear makes unloading workers and pedestrians bear the smell and low flights. Thorough collection reduces this bird’s numbers, but the flock occupying the open water then crowds more densely onto what remains. Providing both unloading-area covers and temporary water outside the pond reduces collisions, but leaves the cost of cleaning water catchments.

### Scenario Connections
In G06-SC1, the lowered water level gathers floating matter into one band; during the migratory-bird week of G06-SC3, that band stretches beneath the bridge. The forced dispersal of G06-SC2 merely disrupts its learned scent route, making the next run more irregular.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/2/display.en: Migratory Wetland Predator Group Spaced Shorebird 'Mudfoot'

/monster_contents/M009/entries/2/bestiar.en: The spaced shorebird 'Mudfoot' sweeps the shallow muddy edge at regular intervals. It has no leader; when a raptor looks down from above, the spacing collapses and the birds take off together.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/2/prose.en:
### Role and Physiology
A common ecological type: a shorebird that sweeps the shallow muddy edge at regular intervals. Its long bill probes for bottom-dwelling organisms, while its eyes first register the distance to neighboring birds and the colors of work vests. It cannot take off from open water; engine noise tells it only direction, and it cannot read electronic guidance.

### Origin
When waterbirds covered the remaining water, shorebirds landed on the exposed mudline and this spaced gait became established. The unpartitioned edge of G06-SC1 is the basis of its form; as the mud extended to the trackside inspection passage, its range began to overlap with pedestrian traffic.

### Habitat
The exposed mudflat beneath Seoul Station’s central records deck and the receding-water edge of the Gangnam Line pond are its main habitats. When the water level is steady, the birds spread farther apart; when it drops sharply, they pack together as far as the inspection-passage ledge. They do not perch on wires or pylons.

### Needs and Economy
It feeds on bottom-dwelling organisms in shallow water; if the mudflat dries or dredging turns over the bottom, its bill probes in vain. Holding the water level steady raises the density of bottom-dwelling life but also increases track incursions. Unilateral drainage expands the mudflat but exposes food all at once, drawing the birds into a crowd.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
When bill tips wear down during the spring stopover, spacing narrows and disputes increase. A flock caught in nets for one season hides deeper in the inspection passage on its next migration at the mere sight of a human silhouette.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
There is no leader; the birds simply maintain their spacing. When waterbirds cover the surface, they are pushed to the edge. When a raptor looks down from a wire, their spacing collapses and they take off together. If H06 combines shorebirds and waterbirds into one count, the HC06 duty officer records the number of birds at the edge separately.

### Escalating Threat
In stage 1, they land only on the mudflat beneath the deck. In stage 2, their spacing extends into the trackside inspection passage, overlapping with workers’ feet. In stage 3, a raptor pursuit sends the flock surging up across the height of the train arrival and departure tracks.

### Combat and Response
Mass netting drives birds that have learned the spacing into alley drains, increasing mistaken captures. It is safer to use zone-specific water levels to keep the mudline outside the tracks and maintain a shallow feeding ground beyond the depot. Success indicators are the number of incursions and the density of bottom-dwelling life.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Creating a new shorebird feeding ground outside the depot reduces crowding at the edge, but shifts the land and dredging burden to another district. Drying the mud to drive the birds out kills bottom-dwelling life and moves the next season’s stopover to the bridge walkway. Giving up one strip of walking space to preserve the mudflat sacrifices a little visibility in exchange for clear tracks.

### Scenario Connections
The zone-specific water levels and outside feeding ground of G06-SC1 are the negotiated solution for this spacing; in G06-SC3, movement along the edge sets off a chain of movements at other heights. Drone dispersal in G06-SC2 breaks the spacing, causing the birds to gather more tightly at the next inspection time.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/3/display.en: Migratory Wetland Predator Group Daytime Hider 'Shade Perch'

/monster_contents/M009/entries/3/bestiar.en: The daytime hider 'Shade Perch' is a small waterbird that stays in the shade of the records deck by day and comes out onto the water only at dusk. It does not lead a flock, competing only for shaded space.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/3/prose.en:
### Role and Body
An ordinary ecological type, this small waterbird stays in the shade beneath the records deck by day and comes out onto the water only at dusk. Its eyes startle first at fluorescent vests and drone silhouettes, while its nose distinguishes human sweat and disinfectant more readily than decay. Under electric lights at night, it loses its bearings and cannot connect itself to a radar blip.

### Origin
When the sluice observation boat became busy during the day, individuals avoiding open water began using the shade beneath the deck as a place to nap. Repeated low-noise inspection windows taught them to take off at dusk, and as fluorescent vests became more common, they retreated deeper into the shade.

### Habitat
Its daytime resting places are the shaded pilings and the space beneath the railings of Seoul Station Central's waterfront records deck; only at dusk does it move to the edge of the Gangnam Line pond. It avoids the bridge walkway and the airspace above the depot tracks at midday, and hides in the shade of rooftop catch basins if the wetland dries out.

### Needs and Economy
It feeds on insects at the water's surface and thin organic films at dusk; shade and low noise are necessary for it to remain. If the deck stays open all day, it moves into the shade along the depot tracks, increasing collision risk. Restricting daytime access, however, delays recordkeeping work.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
If repeatedly startled by fluorescent colors over a season, it begins taking off earlier at dusk, bringing its flights into the peak train period. If its feathers rot in the damp shade, its night flights shorten; after exposure to forced lighting, it hides deeper inside structures at its next stopover.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It does not lead a flock, competing only for shaded spots. Even when the broad-winged roost covers the water, their daytime spaces do not overlap. If H06 reports heat spots in the shade as a bird flock, a person distinguishes by sight whether the birds are resting or taking off.

### Escalating Threat
At stage 1, it stays only in the shade beneath the deck and does not obstruct sightlines. At stage 2, as fluorescent vests become more common, its dusk takeoff veers toward the arrival and departure tracks. At stage 3, its shaded refuge shifts beneath vehicles on the depot tracks, bringing it into the same space as the low-noise inspection window and maintenance workers.

### Combat and Response
Loudspeakers and flashes drive birds in the shade farther under dark vehicle bodies. Toning down vest colors, changing the lighting beneath the deck to indirect light, and keeping drones out of the shaded flight zone delay takeoff. Success means zero maintenance injuries and clear sightlines, not carcasses.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Closing the deck by day to give its shade to the birds delays sluice records; keeping fluorescent colors sends takeoffs toward the tracks. Announcing one hour at dusk as a low-noise window reduces time for recordkeeping work, but means maintenance workers and birds need not share the same shade.

### Scenario Connections
The low-noise inspection window in G06-SC2 sets this bird's takeoff clock, and the crowd inspecting the sluice in G06-SC3 pushes it from the shade toward the depot tracks. The narrow water surface in G06-SC1 draws it to the edge of open water only at dusk.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/4/display.en: Migratory Wetland Predator Group Water-Level Learner 'Pump Time'

/monster_contents/M009/entries/4/bestiar.en: Water-level learner 'Pump Time' is a specialist that reads the band of food on the sloping water surface when the pump runs. It does not direct the flock; it only signals the slope, and a schedule change breaks its learned pattern.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/4/prose.en:
### Role and Body
A specialist waterbird that reads the band of food gathered where the water surface slopes when the pump runs. Its ears distinguish the pump's low rumble from train engines, and its eyes track how fast the water level drops by a handspan. It cannot read the operating schedule itself or know how much water lies beyond a closed sluice.

### Origin
When HC06 began turning on the pump at the same time to improve visibility, it learned within a season that floating matter and fry gathered on the sloping water surface. This is a mechanical clock learned in one season, not a change in migration timing across generations; changing the schedule breaks the learning.

### Habitat
It stays on the water within sight of the Seoul Station Central pump outlet and near the water-level gauge at the Gangnam Line pond. It disperses during the day when the pump is idle. On days when the XT01 wind corridor coincides with pump operation, the slope grows steeper and it follows the food as far as beneath the bridge.

### Needs and Economy
It feeds on organic matter concentrated as the water level falls. Running the pump irregularly breaks its learned pattern and drives the birds toward the pond. Keeping the time fixed stabilizes stopover density but increases the risk of overlap with trains at that hour.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
Once it stores the pump's low rumble as a safety signal for a season, it gathers at the same time on its next migration. If its feathers are damaged by the swift current, it cannot follow the slope and settles at the edge of the waders' area. A single forced drainage brings its arrival the following season forward by a day.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It does not direct the flock; it only signals the slope. Other waterbirds simply gather along that band. Even if H06 raises the density reading on radar, HC06 reassesses pump operation when the pump logs and visual observations disagree.

### Escalating Threat
At stage 1, it gathers in front of the outlet only when the pump runs. At stage 2, that time overlaps with train arrivals and departures, and its takeoff brushes the depot tracks. At stage 3, even after a sudden schedule change, it gathers at the old time, leaving the birds facing empty water as trains pass at a different time.

### Combat and Response
Scattering the birds with a horn binds the pump's low rumble and danger into a single signal, causing chaos every time it runs thereafter. It is safer to use compartmentalized water levels to create a slope only on the side away from the tracks and announce pump times alongside the low-noise window.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Running the pump only by day for the sake of public visibility brings this learned behavior into the pedestrian peak. Tying pump operation to the migratory-bird slowdown period delays freight but keeps the food band and trains from competing for the same minute. Keeping the schedule secret makes recordkeeping easier, but startles birds and maintenance workers at the same time.

### Scenario Connections
The compartmentalized water levels in G06-SC1 divide the slopes this specialist reads, and the timetable change in G06-SC2 brings pump learning into conflict with train learning. Sluice inspections in G06-SC3 run the pump more often, pushing the concentrated band beneath the bridge.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/5/display.en: Migratory Wetland Predator Group Benthic Forager 'Beak Spacing'

/monster_contents/M009/entries/5/bestiar.en: Benthic forager 'Beak Spacing' is a wader that picks benthic organisms from the mud only as deep as its beak can reach. There is no leader setting the foraging order; when waterbirds cover the water, its beak becomes submerged and it stops working.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/5/prose.en:
### Role and Body
A specialist wader that picks benthic organisms from the mud only as deep as its beak can reach. It keeps enough distance from others that their beaks do not overlap, and its eyes look for breathing holes in the bottom rather than water turbidity. Unlike waterbirds sensitive to surface reflections, it relies chiefly on the texture of the mud; it does not understand the numbers on an electronic turbidity meter.

### Origin
When aquatic plants dwindled and only mud remained in a wetland whose restoration had failed, some waders that had searched its edges began following benthic density so consistently that it became a specialization. Once Seoul Station Central began recording turbidity, the success or failure of these beaks appeared alongside the water-quality ledger.

### Habitat
It occupies the shallow mud at Seoul Station Central and the bottom exposed when the Gangnam Line pond recedes. If the water is too high, its beak cannot reach; if it dries completely, the benthic organisms die. It therefore does not go to inland fountains. It does not use pylon perches.

### Needs and Economy
Benthic density is both its food supply and a measure of success. When the pump turns over the bottom, one meal is abundant and the following week is barren. If turbidity stabilizes but benthic organisms continue to decline, that indicates a failure in how the space has been arranged.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
When the tip of its beak wears against stones, its spacing narrows and it drives away neighboring birds. After experiencing dredging for a season, it skips the same mud at its next stopover, leaving only a thin layer of mud along the lip of the inspection passage.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
There is no leader setting the foraging order. Birds merely probe the richest benthic patches first; when waterbirds cover the water, their beaks become submerged and they stop working. Even if H06 increases its wader count, HC06 separately checks benthic density against beak marks.

### Escalating Threat
At stage 1, it probes only the mud in front of the deck. At stage 2, benthic organisms shift to the drain toward the tracks, leaving beak marks on work platforms. At stage 3, after the bottom is overturned, the flock seeks moisture on the bridge walkway, bringing it into the path of passing pedestrians.

### Combat and Response
Removing the mud with an excavator kills the benthic organisms and makes the next season's stopover unpredictable. Leaving, through compartmentalized water levels, only enough depth for beaks to reach and postponing dredging until outside the migration period reduces collisions.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Dredging now for flood preparedness improves sluice safety but diminishes both this specialist's food supply and downstream purification. Preserving benthic organisms to protect the turbidity ledger increases pump work; digging a shallow feeding ground outside the base uses up public land. The choice of which mudflat remains a place to rest must not be obscured by the single label of protection.

### Scenario Connections
The outside feeding ground in G06-SC1 is an alternative mudflat for this beak. Drying the water surface in G06-SC3 kills the benthic organisms, weakening an intermediate stopover on the international migration route. The dispersal in G06-SC2 breaks beak spacing and drives the birds toward the trackside lip.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/6/display.en: Migratory Wetland Predator Group Rodent Tracker 'Pylon Eye'

/monster_contents/M009/entries/6/bestiar.en: Rodent tracker 'Pylon Eye' is a raptor that reads the density of rodents and vulnerable birds from a rail-yard pylon. It gives no commanding call and follows only prey density; it mistakes drone silhouettes for competing predators.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/6/prose.en:
### Role and Body
A specialist raptor that gauges the density of rodents and vulnerable birds from rail-yard pylons and wires. Its eyes pick out small movements in the grass rather than reflections on the water, and its ears distinguish faint rustling in the grass more readily than gunshots. It does not understand electronic lure signals and mistakes drone silhouettes for competing predators.

### Origin
After waterbirds and waders overlapped on a narrow water surface, rodents increased along its edge. Raptors perched on the pylons followed that density until it became a specialization. The airspace above the Gangnam Line depot tracks offered a view for hunting, and in a season without an alternative perch, the tracks overlapped with the hunting ground.

### Habitat
Wires and pylons along the Gangnam Line and high spots around the edge of the Seoul Station Central wetland are its daytime perches. It passes over the water but does not land there. If the wetland dries out, it moves to beacon-like posts in an inland park.

### Needs and Economy
It eats rodents and exhausted small birds, and depends on a short glide between perch and grass. Providing alternative perches away from the tracks reduces collisions along the depot tracks but shifts the locations of rodent predation toward residential areas.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
If a wire spark singes its feathers, its glide shortens and it perches on lower railings. After a season of gunshots, it moves into residential alleys at the sight of a human silhouette alone, shifting the site of predation on the next migration toward residents.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It gives no commanding call and follows only prey density. When waterbirds surge upward, it selects a vulnerable bird at the edge of the confusion. If H06 combines raptors and waterbirds into one score, HC06 records raptor perch time separately.

### Escalating Threat
At stage 1, it watches only rodents from the pylon. At stage 2, it follows the waterbird concentration and makes a glide above the depot tracks, causing the flock to surge upward. At stage 3, without an alternative perch, it shifts its view as far as residential eaves, bringing pedestrians and predation into the same space.

### Combat and Response
Gunfire drives this specialist into alleys, sacrificing both rodent control and public safety. The basic response is to provide a high perch away from the tracks, restrict drone altitude, and collect fishmeal so rodent density remains toward the wetland.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Installing a perch on the wetland's outskirts clears the depot tracks but may shift predation toward homes. Refusing the perch and protecting only sightlines along the tracks leaves collision risk. Removing only the raptors leaves rodents and vulnerable birds along the pond's edge, disrupting wader spacing. No agreement can hold unless it is made public which roofs will fall under the hunting shadow.

### Scenario Connections
The alternative perch in G06-SC1 is the proposed agreement for this specialist, and the pursuit altitude in G06-SC3 produces a chain of collisions. In G06-SC2, dispersal by horn and drone pushes Pylon Eye toward residential areas, making the next timetable more dangerous.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/7/display.en: Migratory Wetland Predator Group First Elite 'Pursuit Wing'

/monster_contents/M009/entries/7/bestiar.en: First elite 'Pursuit Wing' is a raptor whose single glide changes the altitude of an entire waterbird flock, blocking sightlines to the sluice and the arrival and departure tracks. It does not command other raptors; when this one bird moves, use of the space changes.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/7/prose.en:
### Role and Body
The first elite, an adult raptor whose single glide changes the altitude of an entire waterbird flock, blocking sightlines to the sluice and the arrival and departure tracks. Its wings fold to fit between wires, and its eyes select the vulnerable edge of a densely occupied water surface. It cannot read radio signals or dispatch instructions, nor does it know that H06 radar confuses it with balloons and drones.

### Origin
After three functional groups overlapped on the same narrow water surface, an individual that learned the reward of making the flock surge upward with a single pursuit remained as an elite. The overlap in G06-SC1 shaped this bird, and the slowdown window on the depot tracks became an additional hunting time.

### Habitat
It perches on the highest arm of a Gangnam Line pylon and on wires facing the Seoul Station Central sluice. Its daytime hunting ground is the air above the pond; during migratory-bird weeks, the XT01 wind corridor extends it to bridge height.

### Needs and Economy
It eats exhausted small birds and rodents, and one successful pursuit supplies several days' energy. With an alternative perch away from the tracks, its pursuit angle misses the water; without one, the arrival and departure tracks become a glide path.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
If wires tear its feathers, its pursuit misses and drives the flock even higher. An individual caught in a net and released during a season learns that human silhouettes interfere with hunting and begins gliding earlier when workers appear.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It does not command other raptors. The whole of its hierarchy is that this one bird's movement changes how waterbirds and waders use the space. Even if H06 raises its hostility score, an HC06 human decides whether work stops.

### Escalating Threat
At stage 1, it only surveys prey density from the pylon. At stage 2, one pursuit triggers a chain of takeoffs that obscures sightlines to the sluice. At stage 3, the same collision recurs three times, making it impossible to open the arrival and departure tracks without a seasonal operating agreement.

### Combat and Response
Shooting this bird down increases rodents and makes the remaining raptors' pursuits more erratic. The basic response is to turn its glide angle toward the wetland with an outlying perch, remove drones from that altitude, and return the low-noise window to the last agreed time. Success is zero collisions and an adequate rate of clear sightlines.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Removing the elite opens sightlines immediately, but downstream rodents and vulnerable birds then disturb the wetland's edges. Placing a perch toward the residential area puts roofs beneath the hunting shadow. Tying slowdowns and compartmentalized water levels into one ledger keeps the pursuit angle over the wetland; freight is delayed, but one bird's glide no longer blocks the city.

### Scenario Connections
The raptor pursuit in G06-SC1 is this elite's mechanism. In G06-SC2, it learns the slowdown time as a hunting time, and the chain reaction at different heights in G06-SC3 begins with these wings.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/8/display.en: Migratory Wetland Predator Group Second Elite 'Slowdown Signal'

/monster_contents/M009/entries/8/bestiar.en: Second elite 'Slowdown Signal' is a waterbird that has stored the rail yard's slowdown window as a safe takeoff signal. Without commanding the flock, it draws nearby waterbirds after it when it takes off, and mistakes tracks left empty after the slowdown is removed for safety.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/8/prose.en:
### Role and Body
The second elite, an adult waterbird that has stored the rail yard's slowdown window as a safe takeoff signal. Its ears distinguish the friction of slowing wheels from a horn, and its eyes watch the flock settle lower on the water at that moment. It cannot read a new timetable, and it mistakes tracks left empty after the slowdown is removed for safety.

### Origin
During a season when the Gangnam Line slowed at the same minute, this bird gained the reward of taking off without meeting a train and retained that minute in its body. The changed slowdown in G06-SC2 exposed this elite; a raptor learned to hunt at the same minute, bringing the two learned patterns into conflict.

### Habitat
It occupies the water of the Gangnam Line drainage pond facing the arrival and departure tracks. It gathers densely only on days with a slowdown window and does not use this signal on the water by the Seoul Station Central deck. During XT01 migration weeks, the same learning spreads to the bridge slowdown section.

### Needs and Economy
More than food, a safe takeoff time is the resource it needs to preserve. Restoring the slowdown makes collisions easier to predict but delays evacuation and freight. Breaking that minute with horns and drones makes it distrust all subsequent operating signals.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
If the slowdown is mistimed three times in a season, its takeoffs become irregular and it crosses the depot tracks at any hour. If the pressure wave from sudden braking damages its feathers, it tries to take off earlier in that same minute. After forced dispersal, it even mistakes inspection time for safety.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
It does not command the flock, but nearby waterbirds follow when it takes off. If Pursuit Wing uses that takeoff to hunt, their altitudes overlap. Even if H06 reports them all together on radar, the Gangnam Line operations manager decides whether to restore the slowdown.

### Escalating Threat
At stage 1, it takes off from the pond only at the old slowdown minute. At stage 2, it falls out of step with the new timetable and surges over inspection workers' heads. At stage 3, after horn-driven dispersal, it treats every operating sound as a takeoff signal and arrivals and departures stop.

### Combat and Response
Horns and drones clear the tracks for the moment but destroy its learned safe time. Restoring the slowdown to the last agreed time, or opening an alternative water surface away from the tracks in time for that minute, makes the next migration more predictable.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
The issue is whether humans may unilaterally erase the safe minute this elite has learned for the sake of operating efficiency. Restoration delays freight; alternative perches and water surfaces require maintenance work; forced dispersal makes collisions during the next migratory-bird week more costly. An agreement will not last even one season if the costs fall only on residents near a particular yard.

### Scenario Connections
G06-SC2 is this elite's principal setting, and the reduced operations under the migratory-bird timetable in G06-SC3 extend the same learning to the bridge. The narrow water surface in G06-SC1 is the backdrop that bends its takeoff angle toward the depot tracks.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/9/display.en: Migratory Wetland Predator Group Stopover Site 'Pond Mirror'

/monster_contents/M009/entries/9/bestiar.en: Stopover site 'Pond Mirror' is a water surface whose still reflection in the Gangnam Line drainage pond serves as the only mirror for an intermediate stopover. It is not a breeding ground but a place whose coordinates disappear if its area shrinks.

/monster_contents/M009/entries/9/prose.en:
### Role · body
A habitat stronghold: the central body of a waterfowl flock that took the calm reflection of the Gangnam Line drainage pond as the only mirror for its stopover. Its eyes read the wind and the train blast from the ripples on the pond's surface, and its feet stood matched to the gaps in the concrete of the pond's lip. It could not stay long on the flowing water by the sluice, which it did not take for a mirror, and it could not see the electronic water-level alarms.

### Origin
After the scattered Han River wetlands were cut off and only the depot drainage ponds kept a set area, the waterfowl traveling the north–south axis fixed this mirror as their stopover coordinate. That it was a stopover and not a breeding ground was the limit of the body, and if the water level dropped sharply, the coordinate vanished.

### Habitat
The whole face of the Gangnam Line drainage pond was the core, and the water surface of the central Seoul Station deck was an auxiliary mirror. In the weeks when the XT01 wind corridor opened, the coordinate was briefly reflected overlapping from the pond onto the bridge water, and if the pond was drained the flock scattered to inland fountains and the stronghold collapsed.

### Needs · economy
The calm water area, the turbidity, and the takeoff distance to the lip were the resources that kept it. Emptying the pond to open the sightline let dust, stench, and rodents into the depot, and widening the surface shrank the work space and the walking paths.

### Life · maintenance
If the mirror broke three times in one migration season, the next season's arrival came a day later each time or leaked away to a different catch basin altogether. When droppings piled up on one face and nutrients rose, insects multiplied and called in a bigger flock, and if the spot was not rested the stronghold itself became overcrowded.

### Behavior · hierarchy
It did not own the pond; it only occupied the area. Waders used the mud at the lip and raptors the wires overlooking the pond, and when H06 raised the stronghold's density by one point, HC06 recorded area, turbidity, and intrusion separately.

### Staged threat
At stage 1 it occupied only the pond mirror and did not overlap the train movements. At stage 2 the surface shrank and the takeoffs bent toward the depot tracks. At stage 3 the mirror was drained during the migration weeks, and the flock repeatedly occupied the bridge walkways and the train-movement lines.

### Combat · counter
Draining the pond in one go made the stronghold disappear, but dust and other predators struck the citizens. Opening temporary water surfaces off the tracks, keeping the main mirror's water level in sections, and resting the nutrients under the perches mattered as much as preventing collisions.

### Negotiation · moral choice
Neither an order to empty the wetland mirror for the city's sake nor a declaration stopping the depot for the birds' sake was this stronghold's answer. Only when it was announced how much area would be yielded in which season, and the noise and passage restrictions were not heaped on the waterside residents alone, could zero collisions over two consecutive migration seasons be declared. Removing the stronghold itself to hide a failed restoration weakened the downstream purification and the international migration axis together.

### Scenario links
The water drainage and section expansion of G06-SC3 were the main negotiation of this stronghold, and the section water levels of G06-SC1 divided the mirror by functional group. The timetable of G06-SC2 made the takeoff angles over this mirror trade places with the depot tracks.

/monster_contents/M010/entries/0/bestiar.en: The Surface Outpost 'Open Mirror' is the open face that occupies the shallow surface in front of the central Seoul Station records deck as if it were a body. When the surface folds the outpost disappears with it and shares the daytime seat with the pond mirror.

/monster_contents/M010/entries/0/prose.en:
### Role and Body
As an environmental outpost type, the adult waterfowl with broad feet and water-soaked breast feathers occupied the shallow surface in front of the central Seoul Station Republic of Korea Government waterside records deck as if it were its body. Its eyes first cut surface reflections, work vest colors, and drone silhouettes. Engine noise, gunfire, and warning blasts only reported the distance of danger. It reacted to fishmeal and decay smells but could not read electronic signals, and when the surface folded the outpost vanished with it.

### Origin
As spring and autumn stopovers overlapped in the isolated green belts and failed restoration wetlands of the Han River, Nanji, and Amsa areas, the waterfowl that guarded open surfaces in flocks fixed this spot. The narrowed surface of G06-SC1 is the body prototype, and the breeding ground remains in a separate protected wetland.

### Habitat
Ordinarily it moved between the shallow surface at central Seoul Station and the Seocho Computing Group drainage pond on the Gangnam Line. During seasonal migration it rode the wind path toward the XT01 Imjin River Gate precinct along the north-south axis. When wetlands dried it briefly moved to inland park fountains. The rolling-stock depot pond was only an intermediate stop, not a nest.

### Needs and Economy
Aquatic plants and organic suspended matter were its energy. When HC06 Noryangjin Delivery House unilaterally drained the water level for sluice visibility, this outpost was pushed to the Gangnam Line pond and train collision risk increased. When the water level was held steady the stopover density rose. The shorter the distance between perch, feeding ground, and surface, the longer it stayed.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
It arrived first with the waders in spring and autumn, and only then did the raptors follow once prey density rose. When water level dropped sharply the waterfowl left first and the outpost emptied. When feathers became soaked in turbid water takeoff was delayed and it crossed the yard line longer.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
There was no command system. Open Mirror only occupied open surface in a flock. When H06 Baksol combined radar points into a single hostility score the Noryangjin Delivery House ecology duty officer re-recorded it by surface sector and individual count. When one functional group moved only the space of the other groups changed.

### Phased Threat
In phase 1 waterfowl crowded the narrow surface. In phase 2 waders spread to the trackside edge and raptor pursuit made the flock surge upward. In phase 3 the same collision repeated three times and train slowdown, surface partitioning, and water drainage had to be decided together.

### Combat and Countermeasures
Gunfire and mass netting scattered the flock unpredictably and also lost legitimacy. Sector-by-sector water-level control, fishmeal waste retrieval, and drone altitude limits were the basics. Success was not the number driven off but sluice visibility secured time, zero train-bird collisions, and water turbidity.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Turning the pump more to separate open surface from the mud edge reduced collisions but increased labor and energy. Drying the surface for visibility alone brought dust, stench, and other predators to citizens. Leaving only the waterfowl surface as protected erased the wader edge.

### Scenario Connection
In G06-SC1 this outpost became the floor of overlap among the three functional groups of shallow water, and in G06-SC3 migratory week the surface takeoff on the track crossed the bridge pedestrian path.

/monster_contents/M010/entries/1/bestiar.en: Damage-Learning 'Horn Gold' is the waterfowl whose ear-hole feathers were torn after horn and drone dispersal, leaving only the old slowdown timing as safe. It rose at inspection time mistaking the new low-noise window for noise.

/monster_contents/M010/entries/1/prose.en:
### Role and Body
As a damage-stage type, it was the waterfowl whose ear-hole feathers tore after horn and drone dispersal and whose takeoff rhythm became misaligned. Its eyes still read vest colors and silhouettes but only the engine sound of the old slowdown time remained as a safe signal, and the new timetable's low-noise window sounded like noise. It could not decode electronic signals, and the damaged hearing bundled balloons and trains as the same threat.

### Origin
After the Gangnam Line rolling-stock depot slowdown timing changed, the stopover flock that was immediately dispersed by horn and drone lost the learned safety rule. The forced dispersal of G06-SC2 is the body prototype.

### Habitat
It now clung only to the air above the abolished old slowdown section of track. It did not respond to guidance lights urging return to the central Seoul Station surface and tried to rise at inspection time, colliding with the operating inbound-outbound line.

### Needs and Economy
Its food remained aquatic plants and suspended matter but takeoff misalignment sharply reduced actual intake. Using fishmeal as bait to lure at other times left more irregular collisions. Restoring the low-noise window to the immediately preceding agreed time recovered intake.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
Path changes within one season were the result of learning, so even if feathers regrew the old rhythm returned first. It was distinguished from multi-generation migration timing changes. Culling damaged individuals made the remaining flock distrust all operating signals.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
There was no commander. When a damaged individual rose first the surrounding waterfowl followed. H06 radar easily mistook this rise for a balloon so visual correction was needed.

### Phased Threat
In phase 1 it only spread wings at the old slowdown time. In phase 2 it overlapped the new inspection time and crossed the yard line. In phase 3 repeated dispersal made the next movement completely irregular.

### Combat and Countermeasures
Additional horns and drones fixed the damage. Restoring the low-noise window to the agreed time and opening temporary surface outside the track dispersed takeoff. Success was reduction in emergency braking and near-collision avoidance counts.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Restoring slowdown time made collision prediction easier but delayed evacuation and logistics. Whether to unilaterally erase the safety time accumulated by wild animals for human operating efficiency was the issue among S06, S11, and HC06. Removing only this individual on the grounds of damage made the remaining flock cross the track at stranger times.

### Scenario Connection
The forced dispersal of birds that learned the G06-SC2 train timetable created this damage, and the narrow surface of G06-SC1 pushed damaged individuals further onto the inbound-outbound line.

/monster_contents/M010/entries/2/bestiar.en: Aged Wader 'Late Beak' is the wader whose beak tip is worn and cannot dig deep mud. When the old beak stops the following individuals stop at the same interval and block work paths.

/monster_contents/M010/entries/2/prose.en:
### Role and Body
As an aging-stage type, it was the wader whose beak tip was worn and could not dig deep into mud. Its legs walked the edge at regular intervals but at slow speed. Its eyes sought benthic creatures underfoot rather than the sparkle of shallow water. Accustomed to the slowdown sections of the urban timetable it was insensitive to the irregular water levels of natural wetlands.

### Origin
Individuals that had traveled the central Seoul Station mud edge and Gangnam Line drainage pond lip for many seasons remained, gradually delaying migration timing under prey and climate selection pressure. It was accumulated aging, not learning within one season.

### Habitat
The mud edge where turbidity was low and benthic creatures remained was its roost. When water level was unilaterally drained it walked as far as the exposed trackside inspection passage and overlapped workers. It yielded the center of the surface to waterfowl and guarded only the edge.

### Needs and Economy
Benthic creatures of shallow water were its energy. When turbidity was stable but wader feeding activity alone decreased it was judged a spatial arrangement failure rather than population. Creating a new feeding ground outside the rolling-stock depot reduced edge crowding but incurred land and dredging costs.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
When the beak wore further it abandoned deep mud prey and only skimmed the thin mud of the inspection passage. When pushed from the lead stopover in spring and autumn it could not build sufficient density before raptors appeared.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
Waders only walked at intervals and gave no commands. When the old beak stopped the following individuals stopped at the same interval and blocked work paths. Even when H06 combined it into one score HC06 Noryangjin Delivery House recorded edge individual count separately.

### Phased Threat
In phase 1 it walked only the mud in front of the deck. In phase 2 it spread to the trackside inspection passage. In phase 3 edge movement during migratory week overlapped bridge pedestrian height.

### Combat and Countermeasures
If netting removed only the slow individuals the interval collapsed and the remaining waders rushed the track at once. It was safer to leave separate mud widths by sector water level and adjust no-fishing and no-collection times per functional group. Success was yard-line incursion count and the allowable range of benthic creature density.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Creating a new wader feeding ground outside the rolling-stock depot cleared the track but reduced citizens' walking space and dredging labor. Judging only by appearance and removing slow birds for new ones invited poaching and misidentification. The moment aging was used as a culling reason the edge's purification function was also sold.

### Scenario Connection
The mud edge revealed in G06-SC1 was this beak's stage, and the edge movement of G06-SC3 collided with the bridge pedestrian path at a different height.

/monster_contents/M010/entries/3/bestiar.en: Coexistence Perch 'Outside-Track Roost' is the raptor that learned to sit on alternative perches outside the inbound-outbound line. When waterfowl scattered to partitioned surface it stopped pursuit.

/monster_contents/M010/entries/3/prose.en:
### Role and Body
As a coexistence type, it was the raptor that visually assessed waterfowl and wader density from high wires and steel towers and learned to sit on alternative perches outside the inbound-outbound line. Vision was its main strength. It was sensitive to drone silhouettes and vest colors and took rodent and weak-bird movement as prey cues. It did not understand electronic altitude numbers.

### Origin
After yard-line collisions repeated, when HC06 Noryangjin Delivery House installed perches of different heights on the wetland periphery some raptors tested those spots instead of track wires. The alternative-perch choice of G06-SC1 is the body prototype.

### Habitat
During the day it stayed on the high perch outside the track and only briefly moved to the rolling-stock depot steel tower when waterfowl were pushed onto narrow surface. During XT01 migration week it lowered pursuit altitude over the bridge to this perch height.

### Needs and Economy
Its food was rodents and weak birds. Long use of the alternative perch concentrated droppings on specific surfaces, increasing nutrients and insects so that the next season's stopover flock could grow larger. If perch location was not periodically rested coexistence cost overtook collision prevention.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
When length of stay in one season increased the waterfowl collective-takeoff baseline rose with it. Fixing the spot without measuring insect emergence volume under the perch moved this individual's hunting location to residential-area rodents.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
There was no commander among raptors either. Outside-Track Roost followed density alone and stopped pursuit when waterfowl scattered to partitioned surface. H06 altitude points were recorded as perch stay only after visual distinction of birds and drones.

### Phased Threat
In phase 1 it only looked down on two functional groups from the peripheral perch. In phase 2 one pursuit obscured sluice visibility and the inbound-outbound line. In phase 3 during migratory week it crossed bridge and inbound-outbound line simultaneously at different heights.

### Combat and Countermeasures
Gunfire pushed raptors to residential chimneys. Limiting drone altitude and adjusting perch height to avoid surface takeoff reduced chained emergencies. Success was separation of raptor perch stay from collective takeoff and zero collisions.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Placing the alternative perch on the wetland periphery reduced track collisions but could shift rodent predation locations toward residential areas. Using the yard-line wire as-is let trains sell safety time to the birds. Coexistence was not a declaration that stopped the city for birds but labor that measured nutrients under the perch and rested the location.

### Scenario Connection
The raptor alternative perch of G06-SC1 was this individual's spot, and functional-group perch installation in G06-SC2 plus compartment expansion in G06-SC3 divided pursuit height.

/monster_contents/M010/entries/4/bestiar.en: Daytime Convergence 'Three-Layer Emergency' is the aerial knot where surface takeoff, edge movement, and raptor pursuit overlap on one bridge cross-section at different heights. There was no integrated command or purpose of city attack.

/monster_contents/M010/entries/4/prose.en:
### Role and Body
As scenario boss, it was the convergence emergency body born when waterfowl surface takeoff, wader edge movement, and raptor pursuit overlapped on one bridge cross-section at different heights. It was less a body than an aerial knot where the density of the three functional groups simultaneously exceeded the threshold. Visual stimuli and engine noise tightened the knot. There was no integrated command or purpose to attack the city.

### Origin
During migratory week when large-scale movement toward XT01 and sluice inspection overlapped, repeated occupation of the bridge pedestrian path and rolling-stock depot inbound-outbound line revealed this knot. G06-SC3 is the body prototype.

### Habitat
Its existence locations were the three altitudes of the central Seoul Station sluice observation line, Gangnam Line inbound-outbound line, and Han River bridge airspace. When surface widened and perches diverged the knot loosened. When water level shrank to one side it re-bound the same evening.

### Needs and Economy
The closer the feeding grounds of the three functional groups the longer the knot lasted. When fishmeal waste remained on the surface and wire perches were above the yard line energy flowed toward collision. Feeding the functional groups separately dispersed the knot's maintenance cost.

### Life Cycle and Maintenance
When the same collision repeated three times the knot moved from extermination target to seasonal operating agreement stage. It did not disappear after one safe passage. It loosened only when collision count reached zero and visibility recovery rate was restored for two consecutive migration periods.

### Behavior and Hierarchy
No leader commanded the knot. There was only the sequence in which waterfowl crowded, waders widened, and raptors followed. When H06 raised one hostility score HC06 Noryangjin Delivery House re-divided it by 15-minute occupancy rate per altitude.

### Phased Threat
In phase 1 surface rearrangement gathered the three functional groups on one side. In phase 2 pursuit simultaneously obscured sluice visibility and the inbound-outbound line. In phase 3 repeated track occupation during migratory week forced a choice among operating reduction, compartment expansion, or surface drainage.

### Combat and Countermeasures
Shooting the knot scattered the three functional groups separately so the next collision could not be predicted. Slowdown matched to migratory timetable, alternative perches at different heights, and compartment water level were the axes of response. Success was zero collisions, reduced incursions, sluice visibility, and benthic creature density.

### Negotiation and Moral Choice
Reducing operations slowed evacuation and logistics. Widening surface and perch compartments reduced citizens' walking space and rolling-stock depot work space. Drying the surface brought dust, stench, and other predators. Hiding restoration failure by completely removing the flock weakened downstream purification and the international migratory ecological axis. The content of coexistence was a public promise not to shift costs only onto specific waterside residents.

### Scenario Connection
