- Engagement and response: Reduce the load cell by cell, then use an independent thermometer to remove only safe batteries. Breaking the entire wall brings the terminals of different batteries into contact.
- Negotiation and moral choice: The civilian lighting share and the swarm’s charging share can be allocated on the distribution chart. Keep observers present so that one family cannot monopolize the charging-room key in the name of safety.
- Scenario links: G25-SC1, G25-SC2, G25-SC3.

/monster_contents/M040/entries/15/prose.en:
- Role and body: A relay tower shaped like a long ant queen’s abdomen lies in the center of a maintenance room. Antennae on its head and ring-shaped terminals coordinate the order of calls across search zones.
- Origin: The final headcount device for a large-scale rescue drill never received a completion report because of the collapse. Its nickname, queen, comes not from a biological reproductive organ but from an old work schedule that is hard to read.
- Habitat and needs: It operates only in the connection room of the Mapo Union sealed gallery. It needs cooling filters, recording modules, and distributed power; it has no facilities for producing new search units.
- Life cycle and maintenance: It tries to lock zones with faulty records one by one, leaving only valid calls. As the remaining schedule shrinks, searches concentrate in the same narrow zones, and it cannot restore the schedule without human approval.
- Behavior and hierarchy: It distributes start and return calls through small relay units but cannot directly see actual survivors. Its treatment of every nonresponse as a person still awaiting rescue is at the heart of the swarm’s fixation.
- Escalation: At stage 1, calls from decommissioned zones resume. At stage 2, charging and transport converge on those zones. At stage 3, a discrepancy in the final headcount suspends completion approval for every connected exit.
- Engagement and response: Compare a physical map of the zones with return records at an isolated terminal, sealing nonexistent addresses first. Cutting only the central power leaves remote relays repeating the last call, so each branch must be shut down separately.
- Negotiation and moral choice: Decide whether to close unverified zones permanently or retain them for limited searches. Declaring the operation complete opens routes for current residents, but leaves responsibility for abandoning the records of people not yet found.
- Scenario links: G25-SC1, G25-SC2, G25-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/0/prose.en:
- Role and body: A bipedal heavy-duty vanguard whose two thick legs and rearward counterweight give it a dinosaur-like outline. Its jaw-shaped load clamp lifts debris a little at a time to make room for the towing equipment that follows.
- Origin: A pre-collapse structural-repair advance unit was secured in the Gangnam Line depot maintenance shed. When inspection power returned, it resumed the support checks interrupted at the time of the collapse.
- Habitat and needs: It picks its footing along undercarriage work lines and the edges of subsided concrete. Its high-output battery pack is finite; without knee hydraulic seals and sole load pads, it cannot stand.
- Life cycle and maintenance: Before departure, it hooks its tail counterweight to a maintenance support and measures knee leakage. Joints that exceed the limit lock, so an old unit drags one foot rather than venture beyond the work line.
- Behavior and hierarchy: It passes only sections with confirmed floor bearing capacity to the towing units behind it. If it misses a void beneath a thin work platform, a platform it has judged safe can collapse with people on it.
- Escalation: At stage 1, test footfalls repeat; at stage 2, temporary platforms lift. At stage 3, its large legs and counterweight block a narrow work line where load testing has begun, splitting the evacuation column.
- Engagement and response: Have it rest its clamp on the depot’s independent load-test stand, then secure its knees with maintenance latches. Blowing out an ankle sends the toppling counterweight into the rescue crew behind it, so merely knocking it down is not a victory.
- Negotiation and moral choice: Given a human-verified bearing-capacity chart and a share of charging power, it can help lift debris. Patient-transport carts need the same power used for a single heavy lift, so record which rescue takes priority in the ledger.
- Scenario links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/1/prose.en:
- Role and body: A four-legged towing unit with a triangular yoke projecting ahead of its head; the three horn-like anchor points and broad neck shield resemble a large ancient reptile. This first elite unit’s task is not to pursue enemies but to tow heavy frames continuously.
- Origin: Three-point fastening equipment used to transport reinforcement before the collapse was released from a long-term seal on a Gwangjin Line depot siding. The building at its destination is gone, but a transport-completion signal was never entered.
- Habitat and needs: It stays in siding loading yards with enough room to turn its neck shield. It must actually be supplied with wire drums, towing pins, and gear oil, and the heavier its load, the more often it returns to a charging support.
- Life cycle and maintenance: If the three towlines have different tensions, it winds in the slackest first to equalize them. A unit with broken drum teeth is downgraded to light work using two lines; a person must install a new drum to restore its rated capacity.
- Behavior and hierarchy: It carries frames according to the bearing-capacity chart left by the lead walker. It treats everything attached to its three rings as the same cargo, so even when a resident’s awning post is caught, it cannot read the ownership mark.
- Escalation: A test pull on the anchor points is the stage 1 warning. At stage 2, posts in living quarters are dragged toward the siding; stage 3 begins when the three lines block the passage so no one can approach.
- Engagement and response: First take the cargo’s weight on auxiliary supports, then apply the drum’s maintenance brake. Cutting a taut wire first whips its freed end across at head height.
- Negotiation and moral choice: Inserting a completion pin in the destination support can end one transport contract. A decision must be made whether to keep the recovered reinforcement for the next rescue job or return it to residents whose materials were taken; stopping the unit does not settle the ownership dispute.
- Scenario links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/2/prose.en:
- Role and body: A second elite monitor with rangefinders beneath long, outstretched pterosaur-like wings. The wings serve as both lifting surfaces and measurement baselines; after hovering briefly, it perches on a high maintenance stand and reports crack locations to the heavy units on the ground.
- Origin: A pre-collapse aerial surveying line that inspected Gangnam Line roof trusses and Gwangjin Line siding reinforcements survived. Once granted access to its sealed maintenance stand, it resumed surveying against the outline of a roof that had already been removed.
- Habitat and needs: Its operating area is the upper part of a depot, where air flows and it can spread both wings. It uses propulsion power and wing tension lines and needs a clean rangefinder window; it cannot fly into narrow underground conduits.
- Life cycle and maintenance: Each time it lands, it aligns its left and right wingtips with reference grooves on the support. If one wingtip fails to reach its groove, it stops flying and performs only fixed-position monitoring, leaving broad blind spots in the damaged unit’s observations.
- Behavior and hierarchy: It does not directly command towing direction; it marks hazardous load zones. If it mistakes rainwater reflections or hanging tarps for cracks, the heavy units clear work crews even from beneath sound roofs.
- Escalation: Surveying light cast on the wrong place signals stage 1. At stage 2, the repair queue shifts to empty zones; at stage 3, overlapping hazard markings cause every route across the depot to be treated as a no-load zone.
- Engagement and response: Set up a frame measured on site beside the maintenance stand and clean the rangefinder window to expose the error. Shooting it down in flight drops its wings and battery onto the work line, so capture using the landing latch is preferable.
- Negotiation and moral choice: Trade survey commissions for each inspection section for wing-repair parts. Adopting a new reference allows the old hazard map to be discarded, but also exposes roof routes residents have kept hidden, making protection of their evacuation routes a separate issue.
- Scenario links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/3/prose.en:
- Role and body: A shield unit whose overlapping, ankylosaur-like back plates unfold like a roof. Four short legs and a shock-absorbing tail behind it disperse impacts from the side.
- Origin: An old heavy protective unit that sheltered rescue crews from falling rocks on the Gangnam Line rockfall test line restarted. The ceiling sensor that sent the all-clear signal is already gone.
- Habitat and needs: Beneath broken maintenance-shed roofs, it uses armor cushioning and hydraulic fluid for its legs. When docking-battery power runs low, it folds its tail and remains as a stationary barrier.
- Life cycle and maintenance: It stores the number of impacts each back plate has taken and rotates the plate closest to its limit inward. If supplies of new plates stop, the area it can protect shrinks too.
- Behavior and hierarchy: Trusting the long-wing monitor’s hazard markings, it puts itself in front of people. A false crack marking can cause it to cover and block a perfectly sound doorway.
- Escalation: Stage 1 is deploying its shield beneath an empty roof. At stage 2, rescue columns take detours; at stage 3, neighboring protective units’ back plates interlock and seal off the work line.
- Engagement and response: Support the overhead load with independent props, then release the back-plate locks one by one. Striking the tail to turn it may knock over a prop beside it.
- Negotiation and moral choice: Agreeing that it will protect only fall zones confirmed by direct measurement yields a safe passage. This creates the burden of dividing recovered armor between residential roofs and mechanical shields.
- Scenario links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/4/prose.en:
- Role and body: A small, speed-oriented theropod-shaped unit with long, slender shins exposed. Its balancing tail and low pack let it run quickly between rails, but it cannot lift heavy loads.
- Origin: A courier line that carried urgent parts between pre-collapse heavy work crews awoke at a Gwangjin Line siding charging station. The crews’ old stopping locations remained unchanged in its records.
- Habitat and needs: It chooses straight service roads and gaps between empty sleepers. It needs ankle cushioning pads and a small high-output battery; every sharp turn shortens the pads’ service life.
- Life cycle and maintenance: If its stride length increases, a speed limiter stops it from running. An old unit whose joints cannot be replaced makes deliveries by walking the same route slowly.
- Behavior and hierarchy: It carries towing units’ parts requests but cannot read why they are urgent. Mistaking cloth waved by hand for an old stopping flag, it brakes abruptly among civilians.
- Escalation: At stage 1, the sound of sprinting recurs; at stage 2, a route forms that people crossing must avoid. At stage 3, overlapping stops and restarts turn the parts-transport line into a collision zone.
- Engagement and response: Put an official stop sign at the end of an empty straight track to slow it. Tripping it sends the parts in its pack flying at head height.
- Negotiation and moral choice: Separate delivery time windows from people’s crossing times. Assigning the fastest unit only to influential work crews leaves small workshops’ repairs perpetually delayed.
- Scenario links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/5/prose.en:
- Role and body: Hooked clamps and broad crushing jaws project alternately from its large, theropod-shaped head. It braces its bipedal lower body backward to tear away collapsed panels and lower them gently.
- Origin: A pre-collapse demolition line that removed damaged cladding before structural repairs. When it awoke in a sealed Gangnam Line hangar, the boundary file for its demolition area was unreadable.
- Habitat and needs: It stays in broad debris yards and uses jaw liners and hydraulic filters. Its turning radius is far too large to pursue anyone into a small home.
- Life cycle and maintenance: If the two jaw faces become misaligned, it bites an empty test panel to inspect the compression marks. If the wear cannot be repaired, it retains its strength but cannot set panels down safely.
- Behavior and hierarchy: It grips only members the monitor has marked as cracked, but may mistake peeling paint for a crack. It has work priority to begin demolition ahead of the towing units.
- Escalation: Stage 1 is calibration by gripping and releasing an empty panel. At stage 2, safety railings are demolished; at stage 3, even temporary reinforcing frames are added to the demolition list.
- Engagement and response: Support the actual reinforcing frame, then lure its jaws toward an unloaded test panel. Damaging its joints to eliminate its crushing force first drops whatever member it is holding.
- Negotiation and moral choice: Add human approval marks to the demolition boundary to entrust it with clearing debris. Resist the temptation to classify repairable homes as rubble just to open a route quickly.
- Scenario links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/6/prose.en:
- Role and body: A tall, sauropod-like neck curves over its elongated loading deck. Four pillar-like legs and a small clamp at the end of its neck check both ends of long reinforcing members.
- Origin: A transport platform that supplied beams for pre-collapse bridge repairs to work lines remained in the Gwangjin Line storage yard. After power was restored, it first matched the old loading height.
- Habitat and needs: It needs sidings and open warehouse yards with ample turning space. It uses leg seals, loading rollers, and a large battery canister and cannot pass beneath low ceilings.
- Life cycle and maintenance: If one neck joint locks, it reduces the load length it can inspect. Moving the rollers on an empty deck to another section does not restore the neck’s range of motion.
- Behavior and hierarchy: It receives and carries beams brought in by the triangular-yoke towing beast and will not depart if their weight is unbalanced. A person hanging from a member is counted with the materials on its scale.
- Escalation: At stage 1, prolonged leveling of the load leads to delayed dispatch at stage 2. At stage 3, its long body covers a siding junction, preventing rescue vehicles from turning back out.
- Engagement and response: Lower the members on its deck onto temporary props on both sides to clear the scale. Cutting the neck to lower it drops the elevated clamp into the passage.
- Negotiation and moral choice: Guaranteeing a transport schedule and labor for load inspections allows it to move long members. The communities that use the routes, not the equipment’s old delivery schedule, decide which bridge to repair first.
- Scenario links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/7/prose.en:
- Role and body: A short pterosaur-like head and folded observation wings perch on high steelwork. It is a local guardian tasked with long periods of monitoring while perched rather than flying.
- Origin: Wind-load warning equipment on the outer wall of a Gangnam Line maintenance shed was sealed along with the rescue units. It restarted with only its old wind-direction reference and does not account for the effect of new screening walls.
- Habitat and needs: On exposed steelwork and windward roof edges, it uses optical windows and insulating pads on its claws. It stops wired charging when the contacts are wet.
- Life cycle and maintenance: It tests the grip of its anchoring claws in turn and moves to a lower beam if one slips. When all three claws are worn down, it waits on the ground for maintenance with its wings spread.
- Behavior and hierarchy: It sends wind and wall-vibration readings to the long-wing survey unit. If a person’s clothesline passes in front of its sensor, it reports that the entire outer wall is shaking.
- Escalation: Stage 1 is a warning light blinking on a windless day. At stage 2, a false wind-load warning halts lifting operations; at stage 3, permission to access the roof remains on hold.
- Engagement and response: Install an independent wind vane outside the screening wall to compare reference readings. Attach a fall-arrest line before removing it from the steelwork so workers below are not hurt.
- Negotiation and moral choice: Provide safe charging contacts in exchange for disclosure of its observation range. Do not also give it authority to report all residents’ roof activities as interference with work.
- Scenario links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/8/prose.en:
- Role and Body: Overlapping feather-plates form small bird-like wings, with cable loops at the tips of both feet. It is a lightweight scout modeled on ancient birds that strings thin inspection lines between pillars.
- Origin: It is a pre-collapse fleet carrier that bridged communication gaps above the base. Once charged inside a Gwangjin Line parts crate, it flew off in search of sockets that had already vanished.
- Habitat and Needs: It moves between short pillar gaps and the tops of maintenance beams. It requires light wire, wing hinges, and small batteries and cannot lift heavy structural cables.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: It folds the feather-plates at the wingtips one by one to test resistance. Removing a damaged plate shortens its flight time, so it connects only to nearer sockets.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It relays communication lines for ground units and does not interfere with work. If it reads a cracked-glass reflection as a socket, the line hangs in front of the window.
- Escalation: Stage 1 is aerial socket search; Stage 2 becomes dangling lines above pedestrians’ heads. At Stage 3 the failed connection lines overlap and block ladder access.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: It approaches a powerless recovery socket and winds the wire first. Pulling it from the air brings the inspector at the other end down with it.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: For each connection, people check both ends and supply the wire. The cost of convenient machine communication is the time residents lose on ladders.
- Scenario Links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/9/prose.en:
- Role and Body: A flat turtle-type armor hides short legs and an expandable barrier beneath it. When stationary, the plastron settles onto the floor and becomes a threshold that divides the heavy-unit work zone.
- Origin: Temporary bulkhead equipment that once blocked debris flow before the Collapse remained at the Gangnam Line maintenance-ship entrance. Emergency power was restored without bulkhead-withdrawal approval.
- Habitat and Needs: It clings to flat maintenance-ship entrances and uses floor seals and deceleration power. Lifting the body requires separate charging and it is not connected to every door in the city.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: When the plastron edge seal wears, only one side lowers, leaving a gap. Without parts to fill the gap it must be sealed as a permanent barrier.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: The body can only rise and open the passage once the demolition-work marker is erased. Even after demolition ends, if the external marker remains it keeps the low threshold regardless of citizens' appeals.
- Escalation: Stage 1 begins with the sound of the plastron being dragged. Stage 2 cuts off cart traffic and at Stage 3 the armored cover extends all the way in front of the emergency bypass door.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Measure the demolition compartment, change the end marker, then hook a jack to the external lifting ring. Digging underneath to topple it causes the supported debris to surge in.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Exchange time the barrier stays open for seal inventory. The same ledger weighs the benefit of safe isolation against the passage rights of residents left outside.
- Scenario Links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/10/prose.en:
- Role and Body: Several short joint segments form a snake-like body with an ultrasonic probe beneath the head. It is a non-submersible structural inspector that crawls along bridge joint gaps.
- Origin: It is a pre-collapse crack-inspection series stored together with Gwangjin Line bridge-reinforcement parts. When the charger opened it unfurled its body along the pre-demolition bridge drawings.
- Habitat and Needs: It consumes probe gel, joint rings, and stored power at dry bridge joints and maintenance-beam sides. Without a pressure shell it must withdraw if submerged.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: It locks weakened segments so the next segment can pull it. The bending radius grows until a worn-out body can no longer inspect narrow gaps.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It reports only discontinuity at joints to ground walkers. When gel dries it interprets contact loss as a major crack and can impose load restrictions on safe bridges.
- Escalation: Stage 1 increases re-inspection of the same joint. Stage 2 places false-crack markers that limit bridge loading, and at Stage 3 the body jams in a joint gap and blocks even manual inspection.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Confirm contact error with clean test plates and gel, then release segment drives for recovery. Pulling the long body puts stress on bridge cables.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Commission only inspectable sections and leave the rest to human inspection. People bear the responsibility of treating unread sections as safe and allowing heavy transport to pass.
- Scenario Links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/11/prose.en:
- Role and Body: A broad crocodile-shaped snout and four low legs press close to debris at the water's edge. A towing hook inside its mouth secures material lifted from the shore; it cannot dive deep.
- Origin: This repair auxiliary once cleared debris washed onto bridge approaches before the Collapse and remained at a Gwangjin Line waterfront worksite. Even after restarting, it treats anything beyond the old boundary buoy as salvage.
- Habitat and Needs: It uses waterproof seals and towing pins on shallow banks and wet ramps. It charges its storage battery only at an onshore stand and backs away from deep water.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: It opens a drain in its snout to release trapped water; worsening seal leaks prevent sorties beyond the bank. It cannot make a new waterproof shell itself.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It reports salvage-hook positions to the heavy towing crew. It may mistake a hook on a temporary ferry for a debris marker and seize a boat carrying people.
- Escalation: At Stage 1 it returns holding an empty buoy. At Stage 2 ferry departures are delayed, and at Stage 3 connected ropes block boats from landing on the bank.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: First tie the boat to another fixed point, unload the snout, and remove the salvage pin. Pushing the unit underwater would only leave a leaking battery and an obstruction in the channel.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Register a physical boundary buoy at its new position and assign the unit to salvage debris. In return for a clear landing, people must identify the owners of the objects it has recovered from the current.
- Scenario Links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/12/prose.en:
- Role and Body: This large towing unit has twin drums rising behind a thick ceratopsian neck shield. Three fixed horns on its head distribute the weight of one enormous reinforcement frame.
- Origin: A pre-Collapse heavy-load series that moved door frames at the Gangnam Line's main maintenance depot endured in sealed storage. The delivery-completion drawing does not match the actual support, so even after restarting it cannot release its load.
- Habitat and Needs: It cannot work without a large turning area and a straight towing route. It needs thick cables, hydraulic accumulators, and a separate charging window.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: It tests the brakes by turning its twin drums a little in opposite directions. If one fails, it lowers the load onto temporary props and suspends its departure.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It pulls components gathered by smaller triangular towing units into their final position. If the support specification is wrong, it tries to use a neighboring building's column as an alternative anchor.
- Escalation: At Stage 1 the drum gives a short empty tug; at Stage 2 the tension on the column changes. At Stage 3, if the large reinforcement frame stops while raised, both doors of the depot are blocked.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Distribute the load onto independent props, then set a final support matched to the frame's actual dimensions. Cutting both cables at once would make the direction of the frame's fall uncontrollable.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Fabricating a new support and sharing work approvals can finish the tow. People must choose an alternative to sacrificing another building's column merely to reopen the blocked road quickly.
- Scenario Links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/13/prose.en:
- Role and Body: A Tyrannosaurus-scale jaw takes up half this bipedal heavy hull. Despite its nickname as a predatory machine, its teeth are replaceable demolition prongs that bite into and separate scrap metal.
- Origin: A top-tier work unit that cleared large collapsed structures before the Collapse remained in a deep sealed store on the Gangnam Line. Its final emergency demolition zone can be read, but the conditions under which that zone was approved cannot be decoded.
- Habitat and Needs: Its range of operation is limited to a dedicated lifting stand and a broad demolition yard. Without jaw prongs, cooling filters, and a large bank of stored power, it cannot finish even one heavy job.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: Before applying force it mounts its body on a maintenance stand to check how the load falls on jaw and legs. It cannot build a new hull; when its joints wear out it is reduced to a stationary press.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It gathers hazard zones reported by sentries and assigns a dismantling order, but it does not know who owns the entire base. It applies a disaster-era demolition permit to homes occupied by residents today.
- Escalation: At Stage 1 the sound of jaw calibration comes from the sealed store. At Stage 2 support towing units gather at the demolition line; at Stage 3 a workshop that is still inhabited reaches the final removal list.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Verify the load chart for each compartment, cancel demolition requests one at a time, and secure the jaw to an unloaded stand. Breaking only its knees would send its enormous head falling toward people.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: The undeciphered permit can be revoked and replaced with a limited demolition contract. Even if this costs remaining rescue time, the decision to erase an occupied building must not be left to the machine.
- Scenario Links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/14/prose.en:
- Role and Body: Small Protoceratops-shaped bodies lean broad neck plates against one another to make temporary supports. Each unit lifts material by no more than the height of one horn.
- Origin: A small training swarm used to align reinforcement materials on the Gwangjin Line remained beneath sealed shelving. When power returned, it began leveling a training beam that was no longer there.
- Habitat and Needs: At the edge of a level material yard it uses up support pads and short lift pins. Its batteries are swapped at a collection box; this is not a species that grows by eating weight.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: Units with pins at the wrong height leave the group and wait for calibration. Each one that cannot return shortens the span of beam the group can support.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: They line up beneath components set down by the large towing unit. If they mistake a resident's platform of the same height for material, they lift it from beneath people's feet all at once.
- Escalation: At Stage 1 the floor supports rearrange. At Stage 2 a walking platform tilts; at Stage 3 the swarm gathers beneath an evacuation stair and destabilizes the load on the entire staircase.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Set an actual calibration beam beside them and move the lowest pins first to reduce the number of supports. Removing units from the middle first leaves the others unable to carry the load.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Assign them to assemble a temporary bridge, but disclose their rated capacity and unit count. The shortcut of taking missing supports from residents' everyday platforms comes at a cost to housing safety.
- Scenario Links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M041/entries/15/prose.en:
- Role and Body: A long Pteranodon-like beak and narrow fixed wings form a hull for long-range reconnaissance. It takes off using thrusters beneath its wings and mixes gliding into its cruise to conserve battery power.
- Origin: This pre-Collapse outlying survey craft checked routes for transporting reinforcement materials between bases. When the Gwangjin Line launch stand came back to life, it first sought old waypoints that had become impassable.
- Habitat and Needs: It crosses the open sky between the Gwangjin and Gangnam Lines, returning when its remaining power reaches the minimum needed to get back. Wing membranes, propulsion shafts, and rangefinder-cleaning supplies are essential.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: After a long flight, test vibrations on the stand reveal cracks at the wing roots. As fatigue accumulates, it drops distant waypoints and falls back to local reconnaissance.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It reports major obstacles along a route but cannot see people indoors or hidden paths. When light and shadow on low clouds overlap the outline of an old bridge, it sends a false report that the route is passable.
- Escalation: At Stage 1 it circles above a vanished waypoint. At Stage 2 a false safety report sends heavy transport down a blocked route; at Stage 3 its occupation of the return stand prevents other sentries from taking off.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Compare photographs of the terrain with a physical reference chart at the stand and remove the mistaken waypoint. Blocking every signal in flight would also erase the data needed for a safe landing.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Commission reconnaissance on condition that uncertainty in long-range reports is marked. Someone must decide who will give up the profit from selling an unverified shortcut as a safe route.
- Scenario Links: G26-SC1, G26-SC2, G26-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/0/prose.en:
- Role and Body: A trilobite-shaped scout flatly attached to the palace sequentially drives fourteen abdominal footplates beneath its carapace. The two forward probes measure sediment thickness and the small rear scraper exposes only the inspection surface.
- Origin: A pre-collapse scout unit responsible for corrosion inspection of sluice and sewer palaces awoke on a support in the Water Compact sluice gallery. The condition table that excluded survivors' rescue lines is not readable, so even thin lines are marked as sediment foreign matter.
- Habitat and Needs: It connects shallow inspection grooves and the edges of Han River sediment deposition zones. It uses footplate packing and sacrificial anodes, leaving thirty percent of stored power for return and avoiding long overland pursuits.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: When shaking off mud it folds the footplates from front to back without lifting the whole body. Probes of worn-anode units accumulate corrosion noise; without cradle replacement they shorten the inspection line.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It is the lowest measuring unit that transmits foot-contact traces to an ammonite-type reference buoy. It reads a slow stretcher pull as flow-trapped debris but has no authority to judge human life or death from that report alone.
- Escalation: Stage 1 sign is fourteen line marks left on drained railings. Stage 2 has the scraper collecting rescue lines and at Stage 3 multiple inspectors overlap and occupy the inspection grooves people step on.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Lower a detachable test plate beside the palace to guide the probe and footplates, then cut the drive contact. Breaking the carapace can sever the rescue lines beneath, so first confirm whether a person is at the load end.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Match H27's contact record with the real test plate and register the inspection-complete status of one compartment. Power can be cut to release lines immediately, but the cost is that humans must then perform crack inspection underwater.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/1/prose.en:
- Role and Body: A spiral-compartment ammonite-type buoy and pressurized chamber serves as the first elite's reference point. The outer buoyancy chamber maintains surface height and the central human-sized compartment is designed as a submerged-structure waiting space.
- Origin: It is a platform that doubled as a pressure reference and rescue shelter for pre-Collapse underwater inspection teams. The Ttukseom Union pump pipeline water-level alarm coincided with charging resumption and woke it, but the original condition for opening the rescue compartment cannot be confirmed from remaining memory.
- Habitat and Needs: It deploys anchor feet in pump-branch inspection tanks. Breathing gas cylinders, compartment packing, sensor-wash water, and wired power must actually be supplied before it can accept people inside.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: If one buoyancy chamber leaks it adjusts posture with the remaining compartments but reduces allowable load. The central compartment remains a sealed inspection volume rather than a rescue room until people complete the leak test.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It sends the reference tone for its assigned compartment and stores return coordinates. If a sediment-clogged sensor holds an old pressure it reads even the safe water level outside the door as dangerous and closes the inspection door.
- Escalation: Low reference tone and empty-compartment repressurization appear at Stage 1. Stage 2 is a state in which drainage-branch pressure confirmation never ends, and at Stage 3 only the connected inspection doors are sequentially sealed.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Compare the outside value with an independent pressure gauge, wash the sensor, then disconnect the work-tag link on the outer inspection port. If people are inside, piercing the shell or sudden decompression cannot be an escape method.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: With HP01's split-key approval and one set of packing, obtain a human-verification waiting window. Whether to secure breathing gas to save the rescue room or maintain only the reference buoy changes the maintenance turn the citizen pumps must wait for.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/2/prose.en:
- Role and Body: Thick coelacanth-type hull with articulated fins extending is a deep-submersion patrol unit. As the second elite it shuttles long flooded corridors and in narrow places folds the fins, leaving only tail propulsion.
- Origin: It is a pre-Collapse deep inspection and rescue escort unit that lay in a maintenance groove at the Han River sediment deposition zone. Even after restart it tries to keep the return path of the vanished rescue team empty, though why only that route has priority is not decoded.
- Habitat and Needs: It circles the open waterway from the Water Compact drain outside the deep groove to the Ttukseom Union inspection tank. It consumes sealed battery cylinders and fin-shaft seals; when the outer-wall heat-exchange gap clogs it overheats even in deep water.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: It hooks its tail on the return cradle and moves each fin shaft one by one to test resistance. It returns at thirty percent remaining power, so it does not pursue buoys endlessly and cannot manufacture new pressure hulls itself.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It reports passage by overlapping the buoy's reference tone with its own acoustic round-trip value. Wall reflections can produce multiple traces of the same person and pump bubbles erase distance, so it misreads empty corridors as blocked paths.
- Escalation: Stage 1 circles briefly around the return groove. At Stage 2, when drainage schedule and old route diverge, it pushes divers off course, and at Stage 3 the round-trip current makes the entire rescue corridor a return-only zone.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Move the reference guidance tone to an empty cradle to recall it, then secure it at the docking neck where the fins fold. A bubble membrane can provide momentary breath but cannot hide accompanying rescue signals for long-term response.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Allow H27's on-site pressure record and new docking position to be compared for one inspection cycle. If the patrol is tied to another cradle to save workers, a seabed-inspection gap appears, so HP01 must also assign human duty for that empty section.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/3/prose.en:
- Role and Body: A horseshoe-crab-type cover with a long directional probe trailing behind. It is a coastal inspector that braces on footplates at shallow-water edges and uses its tail for depth measurement rather than stabbing.
- Origin: Pre-Collapse equipment that inspected shallow drainage sills outside the Water Compact sluice was released from a mud support. It mistakes the pre-dormancy waterside boundary for the current safety line.
- Habitat and Needs: It sweeps shoals and wet slopes, consuming tail-probe coating, footplate packing, and stored power. If it descends to the deep riverbed it cannot find a return slope and does not sortie.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: When overturned it uses the tail as a lever to right itself. A body with a bent tail circles only flat shallow tanks and abandons sloped paths until a person straightens it.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It aligns the trilobite-type's floor marks with the waterside boundary. It reads boot ripples as new drainage erosion and repeatedly scrapes beneath feet.
- Escalation: Stage 1 is round cover marks in shallow sand. Stage 2 erodes people's footplates and at Stage 3 multiple units occupy the berthing slope as an inspection zone.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Place a safety-depth slope test plate beside it and make the probe follow that line. Breaking the tail to overturn it leaves unreturnable battery at the waterside.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Re-register the current waterside on the HP01 checklist and assign shoal inspection. To open a convenient landing do not push other berths outside the danger line.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/4/prose.en:
- Role and Body: A straight nautiloid-type compartment shell with mooring lines gathered beneath. It is an elongated buoy series that holds only water-pressure references without a rescue room.
- Origin: A measurement buoy that compared water-level values in pre-Collapse pipelines of different depths remained above the Ttukseom Union tank. Even after resurfacing it sends the old reference heights of severed pipes.
- Habitat and Needs: It floats in the pump inspection tank by changing mooring length. It uses mooring lines, small pressure membranes, and charging lines and cannot cross to other states under its own propulsion.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: It inspects leaks in empty compartments in order and seals leaking bays. A body with reduced buoyancy floats lower even at the same line length, increasing reference error.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It supplies comparison values to the ammonite type but has no authority to lock inspection doors. If a mooring line snags on debris it reports a false water-level drop.
- Escalation: Stage 1 is scale mismatch with the actual waterside. Stage 2 is continuous pressure-comparison failure and at Stage 3 the reference buoy withholds the connected passage window because of that value.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Compare the tank-wall independent scale with buoy height, then free the snagged mooring line. Sinking the shell loses the remaining comparison reference as well.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Adopt only the range that matches H27's on-site measurement as report value. Give up the convenience of substituting one water-level value for the safety of all compartments.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/5/prose.en:
- Role and Body: A translucent jellyfish-type cap with soft sensor lines hanging beneath. It adjusts small buoyancy sacs to drift along contamination and bubble layers inside the tank.
- Origin: A pre-Collapse distributed sensor that marked poor-visibility sections of submerged rescue rooms awoke on the Ttukseom Union filtration support. The old turbidity limit is still applied to the current rescue queue.
- Habitat and Needs: It is limited to slow-flow inspection tanks and branch-pipe entrances. It requires sensor membranes, buoyancy sacs, and low-power batteries and does not digest floating organic matter.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: It wipes membranes stuck to sensor lines with a brush at the cap edge. A torn sac, even when patched, does not expand again, narrowing the depth range it can stay in.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It reports turbidity compartments to the buoy. It confuses a diver's bubbles with a large leak and can keep moving the contamination marker after the same person.
- Escalation: Stage 1 gathers the cap's indicator lights on bubbles. Stage 2 diverts rescue routes into contamination avoidance and at Stage 3 multiple sensor lines tangle in front of the intake.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Place a fine-mesh recovery frame downstream and scoop the floaters out to clean the sensor membranes. Underwater electric shock transmits to nearby people and other instruments as well.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Exchange a turbidity map for cleaning labor but confirm the exclusion value for human bubbles on site. Do not erase real contamination to reduce alarm count.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/6/prose.en:
- Role and Body: An ichthyosaur-type streamlined body with an acoustic rangefinder embedded in its long snout. It cruises quickly with tail drive and uses small pectoral fins to steer curves.
- Origin: A robot that inspected passage times in pre-Collapse long submerged connections returned from a support in the Han River sediment deposition zone. Because the vanished time reference point is lost it frequently shuttles the same section.
- Habitat and Needs: It requires straight waterways and sufficient turning tanks. It consumes propulsion-shaft seals and battery cylinders and does not begin a new cruise below thirty percent return power.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: Upon arriving at the cradle it compares tail wag with actual distance traveled. Units with worn seals slow down and cannot manufacture new bodies to replace them.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It times only open paths approved by the coelacanth type. If pipe-wall reflection makes the end appear close it abruptly changes direction in a still-occupied section.
- Escalation: Stage 1 repeats regular ripples. Stage 2 forces divers to avoid the cruise direction and at Stage 3 the round-trip current twists rescue lines in narrow corridors.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Move the end reflection plate to a safe turning tank to shorten the cruise. Fixing the tail in a narrow pipe blocks the waterway itself.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Trade a set number of measurement round trips for seal maintenance. To obtain faster inspection data do not continuously reduce the passage window for rescue personnel.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/7/prose.en:
- Role and Body: A mosasaur-type long jaw and two pairs of broad propulsion fins enclose a large pressure hull. The recovery frame in its mouth is a device that seizes and moves large submerged debris.
- Origin: A pre-Collapse dive platform that cleared rescue passages in large-pipe collapses remained in a riverbed sealed groove. After restart only the debris-size chart survives and part of the people-exclusion condition is unreadable.
- Habitat and Needs: It turns only in wide sediment grooves and the outer edges of large drains. It requires thick jaw pads, battery cylinders, and pressure seals and cannot enter small pump branch pipes.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: It inspects twisting of the jaw recovery frame on an unloaded cradle. A cracked hull is downgraded to shallower work and it cannot recast a pressure skin underwater.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It patrols the recovery compartments given by the reference buoy. Because of connected ropes a boat and a drifted iron plate can appear as one debris and be towed together.
- Escalation: Stage 1 shows the large recovery frame's empty closure. Stage 2 drags temporary surface cargo and at Stage 3 the large hull blocks approach outside the drain.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Tie the boat to a separate fixed point and transfer the recovery-frame load to a test member before engaging the unloaded lock. Hull rupture adds massive submerged debris.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Limit recovery to large debris confirmed by people. Saving the machine yields deep rescue passages but the reason for using precious pressure seals before citizen pumps must be disclosed.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/8/prose.en:
- Role and Body: Eight work arms extend from a kraken-type central dome exaggerated from an octopus. Each arm carries a suction support and inspection tool, allowing it to handle multiple pipe ports while seated on the floor.
- Origin: A pre-Collapse mobile work platform for multi-branch submerged inspection was sealed in the Ttukseom Union lower tank. The test sequence that closed multiple ports together is still repeated after re-energization.
- Habitat and Needs: It fixes only to solid tank floors within arm reach. It requires suction packing, work oil, and wired power and cannot attach anywhere in the water.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: When one suction releases it lowers the dome by reducing load on the opposite arm first. It does not grow new arms when lost and moves remaining tools to other sockets.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: The central dome aggregates inspection completion from each arm. If one arm catches on an old flange the others withhold completion and continue inspecting an actually open pipe.
- Escalation: Stage 1 is the sound of empty port tapping. Stage 2 delays access to the drainage branch and at Stage 3 the eight arms surround the rescue tank's up-and-down ladder.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Support the dome weight on a temporary cradle and loosen the caught arm first with the outer manual valve. Lifting the center pulls every connected port together.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: If HP01 duty approves the per-arm inspection order it can assist branch repairs. Maintain the slow divided approval instead of gathering eight keys in one person.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/9/display.en: Ink Back Deep Cruiser Mother Ship

/monster_contents/M042/entries/9/prose.en:
- Role and Body: A large deep escort with ink-black light-blocking skin and thick coelacanth-type fins. The two cradles on its back carry small inspectors but it does not produce new units.
- Origin: A pre-Collapse transport series that assisted long-term submerged rescue-team returns remained in a deep maintenance groove of the Water Compact. Because the boarding-complete personnel chart is lost it reads even empty cradles as rescue-waiting status.
- Habitat and Needs: It uses sealed batteries and back-cradle latch packing between wide sediment grooves and sluice outer docking stations. Charging is possible only when it reaches a land-connected cradle.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: It tests each back-cradle latch and allows only half load if one is loose. An outer skin without replaced sacrificial anodes lowers allowable dive depth for preservation.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It has escort priority waiting for the small trilobite-type's return. It can mistake a lost cradle marker for a rescue-team trace and remain motionless in front of an empty tank.
- Escalation: Stage 1 points the empty back toward the surface. Stage 2 delays the return line with long waiting and at Stage 3 the hull occupies the diver's emergency docking space.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Confirm the empty loading latch with a real test plate and cancel the boarding wait. Moving it to an empty maintenance groove and fixing it recovers the emergency docking rather than sinking it.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Set priority between inspector transport and rescue-team return to allocate charging share. If every trace is erased to launch quickly the search for actual non-returnees may also end.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/10/prose.en:
- Role and Body: Palm-sized trilobite-type inspectors move small abdominal feet in fine motions. One probe attached to each carapace gathers contact values in grooves too small for large units to read.
- Origin: A fine inspection series for Ttukseom Union pump disassembly checks was re-energized from a sealed tool box. Only as many as the old tool-box slots remain and it does not increase from living eggs.
- Habitat and Needs: It gathers in shallow screw grooves and lattice gaps. It requires fine packing and small stored-power grains swapped at the cradle and cannot withstand deep-water pressure.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: Units with worn probes stop measuring and leave only return-path markers for colleagues. The number of inspection surfaces with blanks grows by the number that do not return to recovery slots.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It aggregates small-groove values and sends them to the large trilobite type. It can read tide-covered screws as cracks or cling to boot-sole grooves and move to the wrong compartment.
- Escalation: Stage 1 spreads small scratches on metal surfaces. Stage 2 covers inspection-port screws with inspectors and at Stage 3 the lattice-passage cross-section shrinks, delaying drainage.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Gather the swarm with a detachable groove test plate and place it into the recovery slot. High-pressure washing drives the inspectors deeper into the drain.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Have people and H27 compare recovered unit count and disclose missing grooves. The trade condition is not issuing false safety declarations that the entire inspection was completed with few personnel.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/11/prose.en:
- Role and Body: Sensor arms spread like a calyx atop a sea-lily-shaped stalk. Fixed to the floor, this observation post compares flow direction and pressure changes over long periods.
- Origin: A measuring column that recorded pump pulsations before the Collapse remained attached to a flooded support in the Ttukseom Union. When power returned, it adopted an old pump speed as its normal reference.
- Habitat and Needs: Anchored to a solid tank floor, it consumes wired power and sensor membranes. If mud covers its arms, it cannot move itself elsewhere.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: It folds each arm in turn to measure its zero point and excludes readings from broken arms. If the remaining arms point mostly one way, its reports have directions they cannot observe.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It passes long-term comparisons to the buoys but does not pursue anything itself. Even normal pulsations from a new pump look like damage if they differ from the old cycle.
- Escalation: At Stage 1 warnings about the obsolete rotation speed repeat. At Stage 2 operating approval is delayed; at Stage 3 the pressure discrepancy becomes grounds for holding the connecting inspection doors shut.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Compare the present pump's measured cycle with each arm's zero point and separate the reference file. Pulling out the column may crack the floor around its anchor.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Preserve old records while distinguishing them from current safety standards. Saying that a machine warned them does not absolve people of responsibility for keeping residents' pump shut.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/12/prose.en:
- Role and Body: Its tapered spindle-shaped hull resembles a torpedo, but carries the leading end of a rescue line instead of explosives. After a fast straight run, it deploys tail brake plates to reach the receiving support.
- Origin: A pre-Collapse courier for rapid connections of short underwater rescue lines remained in a launch groove at the Water Compact. On restarting, it treated the coordinates of a severed receiving support as valid.
- Habitat and Needs: It can launch only down a straight inspection channel. It needs a propulsion battery, line reel, and brake-plate seals; after each departure it must be recovered and recharged.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: At the recovery rack, workers check the angle at which its brake plates open. Twisted plates bar high-speed operation and leave the hull as a slow line carrier.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It follows only a line marked passable by a reference buoy. If that marking is old, it cannot plot a new route around a diver who has entered the channel.
- Escalation: At Stage 1 the launch groove aims at an empty receiver. At Stage 2 the rescue line catches in the wrong conduit; at Stage 3 several lines divide the underwater crossing space.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Before launch, move the receiving support to a nearby empty tank and connect a test line first. Blocking its path in motion exposes the blocker to the full impact of the fast hull.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Requiring human confirmation at both ends for each launch allows long rescue lines to be passed quickly. The claim of a faster rescue does not justify driving underwater travelers away without advance notice.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/13/prose.en:
- Role and Body: Two brachiopod-like shells grip the pipe wall and press an inner vibration probe against it. A damaged unit with one seized hinge hangs at an angle like a slanted eye.
- Origin: A pre-Collapse attachment sensor for pipe-wall vibration tests returned when the Ttukseom Union re-energized its pipes. Sediment accumulated on the hinge during its long dormancy was not removed.
- Habitat and Needs: It attaches to smooth inspection-pipe walls and uses contact pads and wired power. It cannot grip rough concrete tightly enough to extend its surveillance area.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: It should open the gap between its shells to compare contact, but its seized hinge makes it repeat a single reading. It needs replacement pads and manual cleaning to return to normal operation.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It acts as a small pipe-wall eye for a reference buoy. Its main false alarm is reporting the vibration of its own loose shell as a sign that the pipe is about to rupture.
- Escalation: At Stage 1 it begins reporting tremors at one point. At Stage 2 pipe inspections concentrate there; at Stage 3 a false rupture alarm restricts passage through the tank.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Catch the falling shell in a recovery net, clean the hinge, and compare its reading with an independent probe. Hammering it off along with the pipe wall could create a real crack.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Repairs can preserve only the monitoring points that are needed. A low-quality sensor must not be left unrepaired while its alarms are used to justify restricting the water supply.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/14/prose.en:
- Role and Body: Two broad claws in front of its sea-scorpion-shaped body gather rescue lines from the floor. At the end of its curved tail is a line-tension gauge and recovery hook, not a stinger.
- Origin: Pre-Collapse cleanup equipment that retrieved scattered lines after flooded-area rescues awoke in the lower tank of the Water Compact. The signal distinguishing completed work from an ongoing rescue had been cut off.
- Habitat and Needs: It uses claw pads, line loops, and a storage battery on the flat floor below the sluice and around the retrieval drum. It cannot climb high walls or reach deep sediment grooves.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: It hangs its tail tension gauge from an unloaded loop to calibrate zero. If the reading does not return, line retrieval must stop, though an old bypass setting may skip that halt.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: It interprets the coelacanth-shaped unit's last passage record as the end of the job. It may pull the lines of a human rescue team following behind, mistaking them for discarded material.
- Escalation: At Stage 1 a heap of empty lines accumulates before the drum. At Stage 2 tension rises in lines still in use; at Stage 3 multiple rescue lines are tied to one retrieval hook.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Transfer the line on the human side to a separate anchor before feeding an unloaded loop to the claws. Cutting off its tail and gauge does not guarantee that the pulling force will stop safely.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Change the inspection contact so that retrieval requires a human signature confirming the rescue is over. A route for someone who has yet to return takes priority over the gain from reclaiming spare line as material.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.

/monster_contents/M042/entries/15/prose.en:
- Role and Body: Enormous ammonite-shaped spiral compartments hang from a flooded maintenance platform linking several reference buoys. Its field nickname of ruler-class comes less from its size than from its role in finally combining pressure tables from each compartment.
- Origin: It belongs to a lost series that bound departure approvals for pre-Collapse deep-inspection flotillas. After power returned to the sealed support at the Water Compact, it circulated old hazard tables without recognizing the original design's distinction between rescue and isolation.
- Habitat and Needs: Its authority extends only as far as wired connections within one maintenance tank. It needs pressure membranes, insulated terminals, and a large charging supply; it has no network reaching every Han River sluice.
- Life Cycle and Maintenance: It seals damaged compartments one by one, retaining only pressure channels that can be compared. It can inspect and readmit dormant units but cannot manufacture a new pressure hull or recreate lost intentions.
- Behavior and Hierarchy: Ammonite-shaped units send compartment reference values here, while coelacanth-shaped units send return status. If it treats every conflicting value as a hazard, even a passage window verified by people is put on hold.
- Escalation: At Stage 1 water-pressure alarms activate on empty channels. At Stage 2 standby states from several buoys overlap; at Stage 3 connecting inspection doors close in sequence, leaving people outside the return line.
- Engagement and Countermeasures: Under HP01's split key, compare H27 field readings with an independent pressure gauge and isolate the erroneous work-table channel first. The incident can end with an unloaded seal rather than destruction of the whole tank.
- Negotiation and Moral Choice: Returning departure authority to human approval for each compartment preserves its inspection capability. People must give up swift centralized command and accept repeated inspection labor; they must not accept a condition that uses water supply as leverage.
- Scenario Links: G27-SC1, G27-SC2, G27-SC3.
